News.title: Colombia earthquake – live: People trapped under buildings after 7.4-mag quake
News.content:
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake has struck San Jose del Palmar in Colombia, with the impact also causing major damage in the capital Bogota

An earthquake has rocked the Colombian capital of Bogota and other cities with multiple casualties and "significant damage" to buildings reported.

Witnesses said they had felt the tremor, which had its epicentre in San Jose del Palmar, at the border with Venezuela 300 miles away. The earthquake measured 7.4 on the Richter Scale, according to the Colombian geological service.

It said the earthquake occurred at a depth of around 115km, with several parts of the country impacted, including Medellín - the capital of Colombia's mountainous Antioquia province.

News.title: Woman, 23, found dead in Islington as police arrest six in 'murder' probe
News.content:
Woman, 23, found dead in Islington as police arrest six in 'murder' probe

Four women and two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a woman who was found at a property in Islington, north London

View Image A woman was pronounced dead at a property on Bollinder Place (Image: Google Maps)

Six people have been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a woman in north London.

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called at 9.33am on Thursday following concerns for the welfare of a woman at a property on Bollinder Place, Islington.

Police attended alongside the London Ambulance Service and found an unresponsive 23-year-old woman. She was sadly pronounced dead at the scene despite the efforts of medical professionals.

At the scene, officers arrested four women – aged 20, 21, 23 and 26 – and two men – aged 21 and 24 – on suspicion of murder. They have all since been released on bail while inquiries continue.

Police said efforts are ongoing to trace the woman’s next-of kin.

Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart said that early indications suggest it was an "isolated incident". He stated: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young woman who has lost her life.

“We understand that news of an incident like this will cause concern within the local community. Local officers will continue to be visible in the area and are available to speak with residents who have questions or concerns.

“While enquiries remain ongoing, information available to us at this stage indicates this was an isolated incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”

Detective Chief Inspector Paul Waller, who is leading the investigation, says that police are keen to speak to anyone who may have information to help the investigation.

He said: “Our investigation is progressing at pace and detectives are working to establish exactly what happened in the time leading up to this woman’s death.

“A number of people were arrested at the scene and have since been released on bail while enquiries continue. Officers have been carrying out forensic examinations, reviewing available evidence and speaking to witnesses to build a full picture of the circumstances.

“We are keen to hear from anyone who may have information that could assist our investigation. No matter how insignificant it may seem, I would urge anyone with information to come forward and speak with us.”

Article continues below

Anyone who can help is urged to contact police on 101, quoting reference 3700/06AUG. Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: New Lansoprazole and Omeprazole warning to anyone who takes them for reflux
News.content:
New Lansoprazole and Omeprazole warning to anyone who takes them for reflux

ITV’s This Morning and Lorraine GP Amir Khan gave a side effects alert - and advised to call doctor if concerned

View Image Dr Amir Khan warned about the side effects of a number of common drugs (Image: doctoramirkhan/instagram)

An NHS GP and TV doctor has given advice to people who take certain medications. Amir Khan who has appeared on ITV’s This Morning and Lorraine said people need to watch out for the side effects of certain prescriptions.

‌



And in a new post on Instagram, he looked at five of the most commonly prescribed medications. He explained: “When we prescribe medication, in our heads, we’re always weighing up potential benefits versus risk of side effects. And we only give them when the benefits outweigh any risk.

‌



“But if you’re taking medication, having problems with them, don’t just stop taking them. Come and talk to us because we often have lots of alternatives that we can give you.”

‌



Dr Khan said that metformin, which is commonly used for treating type 2 diabetes can impact on the stomach. He said: “It works really well. But especially when you first start it, it can cause diarrhoea, bloating, stomach cramps, and nausea. For many people, these symptoms settle after a few weeks. So don’t lose hope too quickly, but there are alternatives should you need it.”

Lansoprazole and Omeprazole are proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that lowers the amount of acid your stomach makes. It treats acid reflux, GERD, stomach and duodenal ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and hypersecretory conditions like Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. It is also paired with antibiotics to clear H. pylori bacteria infections and prevents ulcers caused by NSAID painkillers.

‌



He said: “Brilliant medication for acid reflux and protecting the stomach, but if you’re taking them for months or years, they can reduce absorption of nutrients like vitamin B12 and magnesium. So they should be reviewed from time to time. Make sure you still need them and that you’re on the lowest possible dose to manage your symptoms.”

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Dr Khan then highlighted ferrous sulfate. He said: ”These are the iron tablets. They’re fantastic at treating iron deficiency, but they can cause constipation, tummy discomfort, and nausea. And yes, they turn your poo black, but that’s expected. So, don’t panic about that one. If you’re struggling with them, come and speak to them. There’s liquid iron that we can prescribe for you.”

Article continues below

On Bisoprolol he said: “We use this for things like high blood pressure. pressure, heart problems, and palpitations because it slows down the heart. Some people notice they’re more tired than usual, feel dizzy when they stand up, or have cold hands and feet. Come and talk to us.”

Ramipril and amlodipine warning to anyone who takes them for blood pressure READ MORE :

Dr Khan said Salbutamol inhalers can: “Make your hands feel a bit shaky or make your heart race for a short while after you’ve used it. That’s a well-recognised side effect. But if you’re needing your blue inhaler regularly, that’s actually a sign that your asthma may may not be as well controlled as it could be and it’s worth getting it reviewed. The most important thing is this. If you’re getting side effects from your medicine, don’t suffer in silence and don’t just suddenly stop taking them without speaking to your GP, nurse, or pharmacist. Very often, we can adjust the dose, change how you take it, or find an alternative that suits you better.”

In all cases Dr Khan said any concerns you should take up with your GP.

News.title: Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf's latest scheme unveiled after botched relaunch
News.content:
Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf's latest scheme unveiled after botched relaunch

After enduring a disastrous week where their plans fell spectacularly flat, Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf were back for more - this time accompanied by a not-so-detailed 16 page document

View 2 Images Nigel Farage is having a torrid time at the moment (Image: James Manning/PA Wire)

Nigel Farage is having a torrid time at the moment.

‌



He and his party face multiple sleaze allegations and he's going through the indignity of battling with a bin in a badly-thought-through by-election. But like an injured hippo with a hungry lion bearing down on it, this is when he could be at his most dangerous.

‌



Last week's attempt to recapture the old magic - and turn around a slump in the polls - fell pretty flat. First he attempted to sell a headline-grabbing plan to use the Royal Navy in the Channel to stop small boats. That was swiftly shot down by the French government, who branded it a violation of its sovereignty that would not be tolerated.

‌



A few days later, home affairs chief Zia Yusuf had another go, this time announcing plans to jail bosses who employ staff with no right to work in the UK. But that went awry too, with the Reform frontbencher branded a "pillock" because Labour has already passed legislation to do exactly what he proposed.

Wes Streeting gives classy response after radio caller's homophobic rant READ MORE :

MP Rupert Lowe skewered as he flaps over whether King Charles is a white British man READ MORE :

View 2 Images The dynamic duo are back for their latest caper (Image: James Manning/PA Wire)

So aiming for a third time lucky, the double act of Farage and Yusuf returned to a London hotel to unveil their latest caper. The duo have spent the last few days drawing up plans to dispatch foreign prisoners to countries like El Salvador or Kosovo that are happy to house them. Donald Trump has done something similar in the US.

‌



A document with the details - such as they are - clocked in at a whopping 16 pages. And that's if you count the title page, contents and end notes. But at least the ink was dry as they got handed out to journalists after Mr Farage got started.

So, not the most detailed plan, it's fair to say. But that's not the point - as long as people are talking about small boats and prisons, they're not talking about the £5million 'gift' Mr Farage accepted but did not declare, or a police investigation around Reform donations.

Which suits Mr Farage just fine. He and Mr Yusuf claimed that once they have served their sentences, criminals sent overseas will not be allowed back into the UK. But how they're going to achieve that if countries don't want to take back dangerous people if they don't have to.

‌



Pressed on this point by Channel 4 News, the home affairs chief said: "So the direct answer to your question comes down to negotiations with those foreign governments."

Excellent, cheers for clearing that up. Later this year, we learned, former Tory deputy chairman Lee Anderson will be part of a delegation that goes over to El Salvador to start sounding out a prisoner deal.

Despite the early stage that any talks are at, Reform's document confidently says it costs half as much to house a foreign criminal there than it does in the UK. Naturally there was no opportunity for The Mirror to question Mr Farage on this, although for the second week his former advisor Raheem Kassam was invited to ask one, this time about how badly the Reform boss is treated by the media.

‌



Now Mr Farage is in trouble, it is understandable that he retreats to his safe space - immigration - where he knows he can get a message across.

But in a telling moment, a reporter from Bloomberg asked when we might hear more on things like trade, foreign policy, defence. As any DJ will tell you, you can't play the same playlist every week.

"Are there more gaps to be filled?" Mr Farage answered. "Yes, there are, but it's very much a work in progress, and we will be ready (if an early general election is called)."

Article continues below

There was a time when Mr Farage would take a question from every reporter in the room. But those days are long gone, with the Reform leader abruptly calling the press conference to an end without calling The Mirror, The Guardian or The Times, among others.

He will be pleased not to have been asked about the gift from Mr Harborne, or the by-election he faces on Thursday where his main rival will be Count Binface. If he gets through that - as expected - a Parliamentary standards probe into Mr Harborne's generosity toward the Reform leader is expected to reopen.

That sets up the intriguing possibility of another by-election if he is found to have broken the rules. If times continue to be tricky, we can probably expect to hear a lot more rushed ideas on immigration and policing over the coming weeks.

News.title: Domestic violence victim says she was attacked in Travelodge after abuser given room key
News.content:
Domestic violence victim says she was attacked in Travelodge after abuser given room key

The domestic violence victim, who has not been named, booked a room at the hotel for a "night away from the fear" after a period of abuse - but her attacker was reportedly given access by reception staff

View 2 Images A spokesperson for Travelodge said "customer safety and security is - and remains - a priority for us" (Image: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

A woman who says she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge staff gave her attacker a key card has described it as one of the most "traumatic nights" of her life.

The domestic violence victim, who has not been named, booked a room at the hotel for a "night away from the fear" after a period of abuse. But her attacker was reportedly given access by reception staff.

She told the BBC: "He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on." The woman said she was staying at a Travelodge in London in October last year when she was attacked in her room.

Staff handed the man a key and directed him to her room, she added. Once inside, he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone, the woman said. She managed to convince him to leave, but he returned and became more aggressive.

She said: "Not long afterwards, I heard him knocking at the door. He was banging, shouting. He was just getting more and more aggressive. I was terrified. I was hoping that he was going to stop, but instead, he kicked the hotel room door completely off the hinges."

View 2 Images The woman said she booked a room at the hotel for a "night away from the fear" after a period of abuse (Image: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock)

The woman revealed her trauma after learning of an unrelated case in which staff gave a key to a man who was able to attack a woman as she slept. Kyran Smith, 29, lied to reception, claiming he was the victim’s boyfriend and the hotel staff handed over the key card and her room number.

He then entered her room in the early hours and sexually assaulted her while she was asleep. When the victim, who is now in her 30s and cannot be named for legal reasons, reported the attack to the staff in the morning they offered her a £30 refund.

Smith, from Staines, was jailed for seven years and six months for trespass with intent to commit a relevant sexual offence and sexual assault on January 23.

Responding to the reports made by the latest victim, a Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the significant distress experienced by the customer and we apologise for the way the incident has been handled.

"Customer safety and security is - and remains - a priority for us. Any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that this should not have happened. Our room access security policies at the time were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.

"Earlier this year, we made changes to strengthen our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures, supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues."

It is understood the individual provided the guest's full name and room number at reception. Travelodge chief executive Jo Boydell previously said immediate changes were made to its room access security policy after Smith was sentenced for the 2022 attack.

But Freddie van Mierlo, MP for Thame, Oxfordshire, where the chain's head office is based, said changes have not gone far enough and called on Ms Boydell to step down. He told BBC Breakfast that Travelodge cannot thrive if it cannot "get to grips with the most basic of responsibilities", adding it needs to make "wholesale deep changes" to how it operates.

Mr van Mierlo said: "If a company is failing in its most basic duty to look after the safety of its guests, and we've heard the most horrific cases come forward, undermining the trust in the hotel industry, we've seen women, people feeling unable to stay in a hotel into the future, I think that does require accountability."

Article continues below

He added: "I don't think the changes that have taken place to date have been sufficient, that's evident, and that's why I think there needs to be a change at the top, because, ultimately, culture and safety needs to come from the very top of the company."

In line with the changes, explicit permission is now required from guests before additional or replacement keys are issued for their room. It builds on Travelodge's existing policy to never confirm to a third party that a guest is staying at one of its hotels.

News.title: WWII veteran who dodged death with a pint of Guinness celebrates 100th birthday
News.content:
WWII veteran who dodged death with a pint of Guinness celebrates 100th birthday

Ken Pusey, who dodged death in 1944 while serving with the Royal Engineers, toasted the milestone with a pint of the black stuff - more than 80 years after it saved his life

View 3 Images Ken Pusey planned to go to the cinema in Belgium in 1944 - but chose to have a pint of Guinness instead

A World War Two soldier who said a pint of Guinness saved his life from a Nazi rocket attack in Belgium when he was just a teenager has celebrated his 100th birthday.

Ken Pusey, who dodged death in 1944 while serving with the Royal Engineers, toasted the milestone with a pint of the black stuff. The veteran received a card from the King and Queen, and a special box of goodies from Guinness.

The life-long Wycombe Wanderers fan also received a personalised first team shirt with his name and "100" written on it from staff, which was signed by the squad. Ken was just 18 when he planned to spend the day at a cinema in Belgium on December 16 1944 - the first day of the “Battle of the Bulge”.

View 3 Images Ken joined the Army in 1944 and served in Belgium and Germany, before demobbing in 1947

Gianni Infantino cornered as three federations pile pressure on under-fire FIFA boss READ MORE :

Russia burns and 12 dead as Ukraine launches huge strike 1,000 miles from Kyiv READ MORE :

But at the very last minute he changed his mind and headed to a new club after hearing it was serving draught Guinness. While Ken was enjoying his drink, the nearby Cinema Rex in Antwerp took a direct hit from a Nazi V2 rocket.

Ken said: "I’m now 100 and I can’t help but look back on the moments that shaped my life, and that day in Antwerp which has lived with me forever. I have often thought about how differently my life could have turned out.

"It was a lucky escape that gave me the chance to come home, build a life, have a beautiful family and experience so many wonderful things over the years. I have never taken that gift for granted. I know life can change in an instant and that you must appreciate every day.”

View 3 Images Ken celebrated his 100th birthday with a box of goodies from Guinness and a pint of the black stuff

More than 1,000 people were inside the cinema in 1944, with 567 killed including 296 Allied service personnel. Ken said: “The chaps had no chance, they were annihilated. We just thanked our blessings, because but for the toss of a coin and a pint of Guinness, we’d have been dead.”

Ken held a special party arranged by staff at Royal Star & Garter home in High Wycombe, Bucks., where he has lived since 2022. The great-grandfather was born in High Wycombe in 1926.

He was 13 when war was declared and left school at 14 to work at a firm which produced instruments for the Armed Forces. He joined the Army in 1944 and served in Belgium and Germany, before demobbing in 1947.

Ken went on to work on the floors of several factories. He had a son and daughter with his wife Pam, and the couple also fostered many children. Among those present at Ken’s party was his sister Doreen, who is also a resident at the home.

Article continues below

Ken said: “Reaching 100 is very special, and the staff made it a day I will never forget." Speaking in 2024 about the blast, he said: “A lot of us were given a day pass, and we were taken by lorry up to the main town centre.

"It was suggested we go to the cinema, or a new NAAFI called The 21 Club, which was selling draught Guinness by the pint, which was unheard of, for thruppence. We didn’t know what to do so we tossed a coin. It came down tails and we went to the club.

"After an hour or so we heard an enormous explosion. We thought ‘what the hell is that?’ But it was just another incident. There was a war going on and people were getting killed all over the place. We didn’t find out until a lot later that a rocket had been fired from Holland and it had hit the cinema directly."

News.title: Daniel Kinahan has his own landing inside Irish prison where 'ongoing battle' rages
News.content:
Daniel Kinahan has his own landing inside Irish prison where 'ongoing battle' rages

Daniel Kinahan has been extradited from the UAE and is now remanded in custody at Portlaoise Prison in Ireland after being charged with leading a criminal organisation

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan woke up in an Irish prison this morning (Image: Supplied)

Daniel Kinahan has set foot on Irish soil for the first time in a decade — and he is now having his first full day in an Irish jail where he has an entire landing to himself.

‌



The alleged crime boss, 49, was extradited from the United Arab Emirates before being immediately detained upon touching down at Baldonnel Airfield in Dublin. He was brought before the Special Criminal Court — Ireland's non-jury court that handles serious organised crime and terrorism cases — where he faced charges of heading a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

‌



Dressed in a black tracksuit, Kinahan, who is originally from Dublin, was told that any bail applications would need to be made to the High Court. He replied: "I think we know I won't be getting bail — but thank you so much for explaining that."

‌



He has now been remanded in custody at Portlaoise Prison, with his next court appearance scheduled for October. Should he be convicted, he faces up to 30 years behind bars.

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan (back, right) leaving the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin, where he was remanded in custody charged with directing an organised crime group (Image: Mark Marlow/PA Wire)

So what exactly can Kinahan expect from life inside Ireland's only maximum security prison?

‌



Located in County Laois, roughly an hour's drive south-west of Dublin, Portlaoise Prison houses some of the Republic's most dangerous and high-profile inmates.

The facility holds up to 226 prisoners and has long been the destination of choice for those convicted in connection with serious organised crime — including a number of Kinahan's own associates.

Among them is Sean McGovern, widely described as Kinahan's right-hand man. McGovern was injured during the notorious Regency Hotel attack in Dublin in 2016 — a gangland shooting that triggered a bloody feud between the Kinahan cartel and the rival Hutch gang, leaving more than a dozen people dead.

‌



McGovern, who Kinahan will not be able to interact with, was the first person to be extradited to Ireland from the UAE in connection with the investigation, and pleaded guilty to directing a criminal organisation. He is currently serving his sentence at Portlaoise.

View 6 Images Reports suggest Kinahan will be given a landing to himself (Image: Irish Prison Service)

Kinahan, however, will not be rubbing shoulders with his former associates in the usual sense.

‌



According to reports, a wing that typically houses eight prisoners has been cleared specifically for him. The Irish Mirror say he is on suicide watch and is being monitored 24 hours a day on a landing where he is completely separated from all other prisoners in the jail.

He is expected to spend up to 20 hours a day confined to his cell.

According to reports, he is now on suicide watch and will have to be watched 24 hours a day, and while he is secluded from other inmates, he will have a TV and access to things like Netflix.

‌



Outside his cell, the prison has struggled with serious problems that will make for uncomfortable reading for anyone heading through its gates.

In December, criminologist John Cuffee, who previously worked at the facility, warned that drugs remain a persistent problem.

He told Midlands 103 radio: "A lot of prisoners want to get cured. They want their drug problems put behind them — they will do their best. If we can't keep drugs out of the country and out of your nightclub, your local pub, it is going to manifest in prisons. But it is an ongoing battle, and it is a battle prison staff will face and deal with as it comes up."

‌



View 6 Images A general view of Portlaoise Prison in Co Laois (Image: PA)

Drug seizures at Portlaoise did fall in 2024, with 22 reported incidents — a 55% drop from the 48 recorded the previous year, according to the Irish Penal Reform Trust.

But staff have raised concerns about the methods being used to get contraband inside. Prison officers warned last year that drones were being used to deliver drugs, mobile phones and weapons directly into the jail, with fears that firearms could be among the cargo.

‌



Gabriel Keavney, deputy general secretary of the Prison Officer's Association, said: "There have been over 100 drone deliveries since the beginning of the year. We know there's drugs, we know there's phones, but we're very concerned they may also contain firearms. There's huge concerns for our members."

The authorities have attempted to tackle the problem. Justice minister Jim O'Callaghan announced that wire netting around the prison was being upgraded to steel netting to disrupt drone drops.

View 6 Images Daniel Kinahan has been a wanted man for years

‌



But Keavney said smugglers had already adapted: "What they've done since the steel netting was installed in Portlaoise, they delivered directly to the prison through the ventilation system — so it's impossible to net the entire prison."

The scale of the problem was thrown into sharp relief in 2024 when ten inmates were rushed to hospital after a mass overdose involving a white powder believed to be a synthetic drug that had been smuggled into the facility, leaving several people in a critical condition.

A Prison Officers Association spokesperson said at the time: "Unfortunately we have been saying for some time that the prisons are awash with drugs and no action has been taken by management."

‌



The Irish Prison Service insisted that tackling contraband remained a top priority, saying it had invested in new technology, increased cell searches and was working closely with the Garda Siochana — Ireland's national police force — at both local and national level to prevent items being smuggled in.

Violence has also been a recurring theme at the prison. In early 2023, a drink-fuelled New Year's celebration on one of the landings descended into a brawl.

View 6 Images Portlaoise Prison, Co Laois (Image: PA Images)

‌



Among those said to be involved was Aaron Brady, who was convicted in Ireland in 2020 of the murder of Garda detective Joe Fox — a case that drew significant attention in both Ireland and the UK. Brady was reportedly facing sanctions that would have seen his privileges — including access to the prison shop, phone calls and visits — curtailed as a result.

One of the more surreal episodes in the prison's history came in 2007, when armed robber John Daly managed to call into Liveline — a popular daytime phone-in show on Ireland's national broadcaster RTE — using a smuggled mobile phone.

The stunt caused considerable embarrassment and triggered searches that turned up more than 1,000 contraband items across the cells. Daly was transferred to other prisons before eventually being released — though he was fatally shot later that same year while travelling in a taxi in the Dublin suburb of Finglas.

Article continues below

For Kinahan, the contrast with life in Dubai — where he was understood to have enjoyed luxury properties, access to the boxing world and the trappings of serious wealth — could hardly be more stark.

In 2024, Portlaoise Prison grabbed headlines not just across Ireland, but in the UK as well, after 10 individuals were rushed to hospital following a mass "synthetic drug" overdose. The white powder was believed to have been smuggled into the prison, leaving several people in critical condition.

The Irish Prison Service stated that preventing drugs from entering prison was a top priority, adding in a lengthy statement: "The Irish Prison Service has committed to continuing to invest in new technologies and measures to support our efforts to keep contraband out of prisons.

News.title: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
News.content:
A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France.

They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said.

The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added.

News.title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
News.content:
Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.

In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help.

"It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.

Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.

Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."

Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."

In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.

"We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."

Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently.

"We went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.

It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Andy Smith said.

"I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It beggars belief."

Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".

News.title: Consortium including Jeff Bezos advances talks for stake in Liverpool FC
News.content:
A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.

The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed last month that the group had "expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club".

Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal and had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.

According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256bn (Â£192bn).

FSG, who bought Liverpool in a Â£300m deal in 2010, previously sold a minority stake in the Anfield side to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity.

News.title: Ex-Cambridge professor Jason Arday cancels live event after plagiarism row
News.content:
Jason Arday has cancelled an appearance in London next month, following his resignation as a Cambridge professor in the wake of allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

Arday's talk at the Royal Geographical Society's conference has been "cancelled at the request of the speaker", the organisation said.

He is also no longer listed on the websites of two other scheduled events in the coming months.

Arday - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his early work, but said he was not a "liar" and that the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

He had been due to take part in a "fireside chat" at the Royal Geographical Society's conference in London on 2 September.

Arday's appearance at Topping & Company book shop in Edinburgh on 18 September is no longer listed on the website and has reportedly also been cancelled. The shop declined to comment.

He was also announced as a guest for the Arizona Women's Board Authors' Luncheon on 24 October, but is no longer listed on the event's website.

He is still listed as a speaker for the Stroud Book Festival in Gloucestershire in November.

News.title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
News.content:
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.

It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.

At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."

News.title: Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
News.content:
An asylum seeker who raped a 13-year-old girl after pretending to be a teenager on Snapchat has been jailed.

Abdul Khan attacked the girl in a nature reserve in Clifton, Nottingham, on 14 May last year.

Khan arrived in the UK in the back of a lorry in 2015, Nottingham Crown Court heard, and faces automatic deportation to Afghanistan after he has served two thirds of his sentence.

He was jailed for nine and a half years on Monday after he was convicted of two counts of rape, one count of sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child, meeting a child following grooming and perverting the course of justice.

A four-day trial was told Khan, who is believed to be 28 and already serving a 23-month sentence for sexual communication with a different child in Derbyshire, arranged to meet his victim in woodland after telling her on the Snapchat messaging app he was a 14-year-old boy.

When they met in person and it was clear he was not 14, he tried to appease her by claiming to be 16, the court heard.

After activity that jurors found had been consensual, Khan, of HMP Nottingham, twice raped the girl.

Judge Mark Watson said the victim told her father what had happened and he contacted police.

Khan was then linked to the rapes by a mobile phone seized during his arrest over his contact with the child in Derbyshire.

Yet despite DNA evidence subsequently linking him to the attack, Nottinghamshire Police said he continued to deny having met the victim.

Addressing Khan, the judge said: "You deliberately concealed your true identity. She thought she was communicating with a child of her own age.

"It was a lie you have persisted with throughout these proceedings."

News.title: We should smile at our dogs - a new scientific study reveals why
News.content:
Any dog lover will tell you their canine friend picks up on their mood and emotions.

Now scientists have worked out exactly what is going on inside a dog's brain when it sees a human - even a complete stranger - smiling or scowling.

Their research involved 14 dogs in total who all sat very still in a brain scanner while they were shown pictures of people's faces.

Photographs of happy, smiling human faces made an area of the brain that is associated with reward "light up" with activity.

This reward circuitry is the part of the brain that is activated when we enjoy and remember good things, like tasty food or praise.

In terms of our own brains, we often refer to it as the "dopamine hit" that is triggered by winning a game or even receiving a positive comment on a social media post.

News.title: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
News.content:
Tattoos have been in the cultural mainstream for years. Even the prime minister has got one (a bee, on his bicep).

And there are no signs the trend is starting to fade. More people than ever are going under the needle as a form of self-expression: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, according to a 2024 YouGov poll.

The most popular body part to be inked? The upper arm, says YouGov.

But has that acceptance carried over into the workplace?

News.title: Ban on 'subscription traps' brought forward by three months
News.content:
Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.

The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much higher prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.

It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

News.title: British couple held in Iran end hunger strike
News.content:
A British couple jailed in Iran after being accused of espionage have ended their hunger strikes after 93 and 84 days respectively.

Craig and Lindsay Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while passing through Iran on a motorcycle journey from Europe to Australia. They were both sentenced to 10 years in jail in February, but Craig Foreman's family said his punishment had been extended by two years after speaking to the media.

The couple from East Sussex, who both deny espionage, went on hunger strike in May when prison authorities prevented them from calling their families.

The family of the couple said they had been protesting against how they and other prisoners were being treated.

A spokesperson for the family said the couple agreed with prison guards to end their strike to be able to speak directly to their loved ones again.

However, the family said contact was yet to be re-established, as of Monday afternoon.

The family had also previously called for the couple to end their hunger strike.

Five people outside the prison joined the pair on their hunger strike for the final five days as an act of solidarity, the family added.

The fast ran from Tuesday to Saturday with Lindsay Foreman's son Joe Bennett and four unnamed others taking part in the UK, as well as other prisoners inside Tehran's Evin jail, the family said.

"My mum and Craig have spent months on hunger strike, and even at the point of bringing it to an end they wanted to make it about something bigger than themselves," Bennett, from Folkestone in Kent, said.

"Those final five days became about people standing together around values that should be universal: Truth, justice, kindness, peace and unity."

By the end of the protest, Craig Foreman had been on hunger strike for 93 days, and Lindsay Foreman for 84 days, the family added.

Although they said they were unaware of the condition of the pair, who had consumed just milk and either honey or salt in water during their strikes.

Bennett said the couple also went on a separate hunger striker back in November as a "cry out for help".

News.title: Six arrested after woman found dead in north London
News.content:
Six people have been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a 23-year-old woman in north London.

Police were called at 09:33 BST on Thursday, following concerns for the welfare of a woman at a residential address on Bollinder Place, Clerkenwell.

Officers attended alongside the London Ambulance Service and found an unresponsive woman, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

Four women, aged 20, 21, 23, and 26, and two men, aged 21 and 24 were arrested at the scene. All six have since been released on bail while enquiries continue.

Work is ongoing to trace the woman's next-of-kin, who will be supported by specially trained officers once identified.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young woman who has lost her life.

"We understand that news of an incident like this will cause concern within the local community."

He said that the death appears to be an "isolated incident" with no wider risk to the public but that officers will "continue to be visible in the area".

Det Ch Insp Paul Waller said: "Our investigation is progressing at pace and detectives are working to establish exactly what happened in the time leading up to this woman's death."

He added that detectives want to speak with anyone with information the woman's death.

News.title: Ex-PE teacher who hit children with golf balls ordered to do unpaid work
News.content:
A former PE teacher has been ordered to carry out 300 hours of unpaid work for violent attacks on teenage pupils at a scandal-hit residential school in North Ayrshire.

Michael Neil, 72, locked children in the gym hall and struck them with golf balls at the now-closed Kerelaw in Stevenston between 1991 and 2003.

The ex-footballer, who played for Arbroath and Clyde and Stranraer, carried out so many attacks on pupils that a jury heard he could not even remember them.

At sentencing, Sheriff Eoin McGinty said Neil's pupils had experienced "fear, humiliation and physical harm" - but he decided against a jail sentence for reasons including Neil's "advanced years".

He is the latest former staff member to be convicted of offences at the school and will be supervised for two years.

In 2024, Police Scotland declared a "critical incident" over the scale of its investigation into historical abuse allegations at Kerelaw.

News.title: Radio Caroline breached Ofcom rules after mistakenly announcing King's death
News.content:
Radio Caroline has been found in breach of broadcasting rules after it mistakenly announced the death of King Charles III.

The station aired three pre-recorded announcements falsely stating the King had died during the Barry Marsh Show on 19 May.

The messages claimed the "news media" had "confirmed" the death, and were followed by the national anthem and 16 minutes of silence on DAB+, while AM listeners heard back-up music. A correction and apology was broadcast 30 minutes later.

The ruling by media watchdog Ofcom stated that once the staff member who accidentally played the files realised what they had done, they stopped playing them, "panicked and left the premises".

Ofcom said the incident breached Rule 5.1, which requires news to be reported with due accuracy, and Rule 5.2, which says significant mistakes must be corrected quickly.

It described the false announcement as a "very significant inaccuracy" on a matter of "very high public interest".

The mistake happened after a staff member carrying out maintenance accessed preârecorded obituary files intended for use in the event of the King's death.

Ofcom said the files were played "out of curiosity", cutting off the presenter's remote stream and putting the announcements on air.

News.title: Mars Bar from 1991 found - and it's 20g bigger than one from today
News.content:
A 35-year-old Mars Bar has been found during a house clearance â and the discovery has gone viral amid claims it highlights the effect of "shrinkflation".

The chocolate bar with a best-before date of 1991 was found during a clear-out of a house in Scunthorpe.

Victoria Gordon, who runs the cleaning service, posted a photo on social media of the 62.5g bar alongside one of today's Mars Bars, which is 40g.

"It was nearly as big as my hand, which was kind of why I noticed it," she said.

News.title: Senior detective under investigation over use of AI
News.content:
A senior detective is being investigated over potential artificial intelligence (AI)-related gross misconduct.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had started investigating the officer after they were referred to the watchdog by Derbyshire Police following an "internal review" of their use of AI.

The investigation into the force comes two months after a criminal investigation was launched into another officer accused of using AI systems to "create evidential material in a number of cases".

Derbyshire Police said on Monday it made a voluntary referral to the IOPC on 23 June "regarding an officer's use of artificial intelligence".

The force said the latest investigation was being independently led by the IOPC and it was unable to comment further.

The Financial Times (FT), external reported a person familiar with events said the case involved a detective chief inspector at the force alleged to have used AI to maintain "decision logs".

Senior investigators maintain such logs during investigations to record why they took each step, and they can be disclosed for defence lawyers to scrutinise during court cases, the FT said.

News.title: Thames Water gave finance boss a £1m signing-on fee
News.content:
Thames Water paid its finance chief a Â£1m signing-on fee in July as the company struggles with a mountain of debt and faces temporary nationalisation.

Steve Buck joined the company in April 2025 but it is understood the seven-figure payment was not made until last month after the company had taken legal advice over its contractual obligations.

The existence of the payment, first reported by Sky News,, external was revealed in a letter from the Thames Water chairman to MPs on the Commons Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee.

In the letter,, external Sir Adrian Montague said he understood customers would see large payments to senior leaders as "unjust" but argued they were necessary to stop staff leaving.

The letter said: "The majority of the team were brought in recently to fix the problems the company faces and are not responsible for causing those problems.

"These talented and experienced individuals have opportunities for roles outside Thames Water and, in many cases, have been actively approached by other companies.

"These roles would be less in the public gaze, less difficult and more remunerative."

Sir Adrian described the payment to Buck as a "necessary incentive" and said the money had come from emergency funding provided by Thames Water's lenders.

He said the company is facing recruitment and retention difficulties and warned the problem would "persist" if it was nationalised or put into special administration.

Radio Caroline has been found to have breached Ofcom rules when it accidentally announced that the King had died.

The Essex broadcaster apologised in May after the messages were played on The Barry Marsh Show, one of which said “we have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III”.

The messages were followed by the national anthem and around 16 minutes of silence before the presenter apologised for the error.

He said: “I’ve just been informed that we’ve played in error some information a little earlier. I didn’t hear this myself, but it is incorrect, it’s a technical issue, and of course we apologise.”

An Ofcom ruling said a member of staff carrying out maintenance on the studio computer accessed the pre-recorded sound files and played them out of curiosity, unaware it would lead to the audio being broadcast live.

Once they realised what had happened, they stopped the files and “panicked and left the premises”.

The media regulator said it had received two complaints about the broadcast, and said it had breached rules 5.1, requiring that news is reported accurately and impartially, and 5.2, requiring that mistakes in news are acknowledged and corrected on air quickly.

open image in gallery The Essex radio show apologised in May after the messages were played on The Barry Marsh Show, one of which said 'we have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III' ( Reuters )

An Ofcom statement read: “We considered this to have been a very significant inaccuracy about an issue of particular public importance.

“As outlined above, Radio Caroline did not broadcast an apology and clarification until approximately 30 minutes after the inaccurate announcements were first broadcast.

“We noted that the Licensee was monitoring the output around the time of the incident and that an engineer was already aware of the issue, but that it took some time to understand what had occurred and reinstate the scheduled programme, with that being exacerbated by the circumstances of the presenter streaming the programme remotely.”

The station said the files that contained the messages were accompanied by “a set of strict instructions to presenters and managers” to follow before playing them, but that a member of staff played them out of curiosity.

Radio Caroline said that they “took the matter very seriously”, and that they had acted “as soon as possible”.

open image in gallery Radio Caroline said that they ‘took the matter very seriously’, and that they had acted ‘as soon as possible’ ( AFP/Getty )

The station said the staff member who played the files had been “reprimanded” and had “apologised”, and that in order to prevent a recurrence of this issue, Radio Caroline had removed the relevant files from the desktop on the studio computer.

It also said that its presenters and support staff had been reminded of the relevant procedures.

This article was updated on the day of publication. It originally stated that the presenter had ‘panicked and left the premises’ but that was inaccurate - it was a staff member and not the presenter who did this.

News.content:

Solar eclipses glasses are almost impossible to buy in-store and online – and members of the public have been issued with an urgent warning over trying other techniques.

On the high street and internet stores, eclipses glasses are largely sold out ahead of the celestial spectacle this week.

But members of the public have been warned that counterfeit glasses and other alternative ways of seeing the eclipse could lead to harm.

The caution follows warnings from eye doctors, who emphasise that looking straight at the Sun for even brief periods can cause permanent vision damage.

On August 12, the Moon will obscure over 90 per cent of the Sun between 6.17pm and 8.06pm, representing the greatest coverage seen above the UK since 1999.

Specialists stress that only ISO 12312-2 certified glasses offer safe protection. However, approved products are largely sold out, with remaining options requiring hefty delivery fees for timely arrival.

Experts have warned that so-called eclipse glasses that do not carry the safety standards, or ordinary sunglasses, no matter how dark, should never be worn to view an eclipse, as they reduce glare, making it feel more comfortable to look at the Sun for longer, but still allow harmful solar radiation to reach the retina.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

open image in gallery Specialists stress that only ISO 12312-2 certified glasses offer safe protection. ( AFP/Getty )

Around 40% had looked at it for less than a minute.

Mohamed Elalfy, a consultant ophthalmologist and president of the Royal College of Ophthalmologists, said: “The safest way to enjoy the eclipse is to observe it indirectly, such as by watching a live broadcast.

“Looking directly at the Sun during a solar eclipse can cause damage to the retina, potentially damaging the cells responsible for sharp central vision.

“Crucially, the retina has no pain receptors, so people will not feel the damage as it happens.

“Symptoms may only become apparent several hours later and can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot, distorted vision, reduced colour perception and increased sensitivity to light.

“While some people recover over weeks or months, others can be left with permanent visual impairment.”

Kyla Black, Boots Opticians director of optical practice, urged parents to be “particularly careful” letting their children view the eclipse, and warned some DIY filters can also be dangerous.

“If you’re purchasing specially made eclipse glasses, make sure to double check that they are undamaged before use as even a glimpse of damage could have an impact on your eyesight,” she said.

“It’s a common myth that wearing multiple pairs of sunglasses can protect you from any harmful UV light – this is untrue and should be avoided at all costs as only purpose-built eclipse glasses can allow you to watch an eclipse.”

open image in gallery Special glasses are needed for safely viewing the eclipse. ( AFP/Getty )

Ms Black added: “Although a fun idea for many may be to make DIY filters and pinhole projectors out of cereal boxes, this can also be dangerous.

“Objects such as smoked glass, colour film, floppy disks, X-ray film, and dark sunglasses are unable to block invisible infrared and ultraviolet rays, potentially leading to damage to your eyesight.

“Budding astronomers who will be looking through cameras, binoculars or telescopes at the eclipse must make sure they have approved solar filters attached.

“If you’re not sure your telescope does, then contact the maker of the product to ensure you know you’ll be safe.”

The Royal Observatory Greenwich also warned the public that regular sunglasses are not a safe enough method to view the cosmic phenomenon.

Imo Bell, a planetarium astronomer at the observatory, previously told the Press Association: “It’s not a total eclipse, but over 90% is really exciting.

“We’re not going to get one this good for a really long time.

“So, it’s important not to miss it, and to be prepared.

open image in gallery Celestron solar eclipse glasses on sale at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, ahead of the solar eclipse on August 12 ( Jordan Pettitt/PA )

“You can’t just go out and expect to have a look, because it’s really dangerous for your eyes.

“So, you can use solar eclipse glasses, which are very, very different from sunglasses – they block out so much light that you can’t see anything through them except the Sun, because that’s how much light they need to block for the damaging light of the Sun to be safe to view.

“Ideally a solar telescope is an amazing way to witness it, and if you don’t have one of them then you can look into whether your local astronomy society is doing any events.

“And if all else fails, you can project the image of the eclipse using a household item like a colander which has lots of holes in – point the colander towards the Sun with your back facing it, and in the shadow of the colander you’ll be able to see the eclipse in the holes, which is really cool.”

open image in gallery

In an added bonus for stargazers, the annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak on the night of August 12-13.

The shower is produced as Earth ploughs through a stream of dust left behind by Comet Swift–Tuttle.

Each tiny grain strikes Earth’s atmosphere at about 60 kilometres per second, burning up in a brief flash that takes the appearance of a shooting star.

News.content:

A sightseeing cruise in the New York Harbor ended in catastrophe Saturday night when a small motorboat carrying 14 people capsized near the Statue of Liberty, killing a mother and her 5-month-old daughter.

The passengers, who had gathered to celebrate a birthday, were thrown into the dark water after the vessel overturned, screaming for help as rescuers raced to the scene.

The disaster has prompted a joint Coast Guard and New York City Police Department investigation into what caused the boat to flip — and whether the trip was operating as an unlawful charter. The vessel’s operator has been arrested and charged.

“We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life,” Captain Doreen McCarthy, the Coast Guard Sector New York Commander, said in a press release. “We are committed to holding illegal operators accountable to [the] highest extent of the law.”

open image in gallery A boat carrying 14 people capsized in the New York Harbor on Saturday night, leaving a mother and her 5-month-old infant dead. The vessel operator has since been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment ( Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

What happened?

Fourteen people boarded a 22-foot bowrider at Randall’s Island at about 7 p.m. for a surprise 41st-birthday celebration for Paula Rivera, her 20-year-old daughter, Sara Raez, told The New York Post. The family and friends had chartered the vessel through Zeus Luxury.

Hours after embarking, as the group returned from the Statue of Liberty, the boat — described by the Post as “dangerously overcrowded” — capsized.

“When we were heading back, we were slow, but out of nowhere, people started screaming because the front of the boat went into the water,” Raez told the Post. “The water got into the boat. The boat went up, and when it went down — it was in seconds — it flipped over.”

“Everyone was on the bottom of the boat,” she continued. “We were just trying to get out. Then, when finally everyone got out, everyone was screaming, because we were still missing them, too.”

Some passengers climbed onto the hull of the overturned boat and tried to signal a distant vessel for help, Raez said. A nearby “party boat” eventually came to their aid, throwing life jackets to those in the water.

open image in gallery The boat capsized around 10 pm, after the vessel was on its way back from the Statue of Liberty ( The New York Post )

The Coast Guard, New York City Police Department and New York City Fire Department responded with eight boats and a helicopter.

“While all persons on the overturned vessels were recovered, two of the passengers, a mother and child, were pronounced deceased shortly after recovery,” the Coast Guard said. “The remaining survivors are reported to be in stable condition.”

Adam Schwartz told The Associated Press that his company’s boat, Sea the City II, was in the area when the accident occurred and took on the 12 survivors.

“Our captain and both crew members immediately assisted, called in to the Coast Guard and...then coordinated with the Coast Guard and NYPD Harbor units to bring them to land in Brooklyn,” Schwartz told the outlet.

Who were the victims?

The victims were identified as 27-year-old Sara Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, according to WABC. Both were taken to a local hospital in critical condition and later pronounced dead. Sanchez lived in College Point, Queens.

Among those rescued was Andres Garcia, Sanchez’s partner and Antonella’s father. The Post reported that Garcia was photographed weeping after the rescue.

Raez told the outlet that the couple also have a 6-year-old son, Salvador, who was not on the boat Saturday.

A GoFundMe fundraiser says Garcia suffered “a loss that no husband or father should ever have to endure.”

open image in gallery The victims were identified as 27-year-old Sara Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, according to WABC. Among those rescued was Andres Garcia, Sanchez’s partner and Antonella’s father. The couple also have a 6-year-old son ( GoFundMe )

“No amount of money can replace Sara or Antonella,” the online fundraiser states. “But together, we can give Andres some breathing room to grieve, take care of their son, Salvador, and begin facing a future that changed in an instant.”

“I’m in shock,” Diego Naranjo, a neighbor of the family, told WABC. “For the family, sending condolences to the family. May they rest in peace in heaven.”

Who was charged?

The captain of the 22-foot vessel, 46-year-old Manuel Hernandez, was arrested and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, the Post reported.

“Coast Guard Investigators are also determining whether the operation constitutes an illegal charter operation and are coordinating efforts in conjunction with NYPD,” the Coast Guard said. “An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that lacks required U.S. Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.”

Although 14 people were aboard Saturday night, the boat had a maximum seating capacity of 10, the Post reported, citing police sources. Passengers were not required to wear life jackets, except for 5-month-old Antonella.

The case against Hernandez, who is from Manhattan, has been taken over by federal prosecutors, CNN reported.

Zeus Luxury describes itself as “one of the leading companies in limousine, party bus, and yacht rentals in the tri-state area,” with a fleet that includes “40 high-end vehicles from top brands.”

The Independent has contacted the company for comment.

Swimming pools and car washes are among the UK businesses that could be hit by a water ban as providers look to conserve resources amid drought conditions and an upcoming fifth heatwave.

Southern Water has applied to the government for permission to issue a “non-essential use ban” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. If granted and put into action, the policy would prevent businesses from activities like washing cars with hosepipes, and filling private swimming pools.

It comes as half of England and all of Wales have been plunged into drought and more regions could be declared when officials meet at the National Drought Group on Monday.

open image in gallery Private swimming pools could be banned if the measures go ahead ( Getty )

Temperatures are set to soar to as high as 36C this week as parts of the country face their fifth heatwave this summer.

A Southern Water spokesperson confirmed it had applied for a drought order and a non-essential use ban as a precaution, but that it does not currently plan to enact the measures.

"This isn't a choice between protecting the river and supplying customers,” a Southern Water spokesperson said. “We have to do both. The Drought Order process helps ensure we can maintain essential water supplies during an exceptional drought, while operating within a regulatory framework designed to balance environmental protection with the needs of the communities that rely on the River Test."

Drought was declared across East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the west Midlands, and Wessex on 29 July.

open image in gallery An aerial view shows the dried and cracked bed of the depleted Hollow Pond and Leyton flats near Wanstead, east London ( AFP/Getty )

More than 25 million people have restrictions on water use, the Environment Agency said, with millions under hosepipe bans, including all South East Water and Thames Water customers.

A non-essential use ban comes as part of the next level of drought restriction that applies to business and commercial activities that use large amounts of water but aren't considered essential.

There is no specific date set for the hosepipe bans to end but water companies have explained that it will be lifted once water sources have recovered back to normal levels.

Southern Water has previously said it needs enough water in reservoirs, rivers and underground aquifers to meet demand before it can lift the ban.

Met Office science manager Dr Amy Doherty described July as a “truly remarkable month” in the UK’s climate record.

“The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records,” she said.

Last summer, the government granted two drought orders during a season which saw four heatwaves and the driest August for England since 2003.

News.title: The five simple ways you can cut back on your water usage in a drought

With so much of the world suffering from drought, you might think your ability to help is minimal. But when you consider the average person in the UK uses around 142 litres of water a day, it’s easy to see how small changes to your routine can add up.

More than half of the water that is extracted from rivers, streams and aquifers in the UK feeds the public water supply. These abstractions, as they’re called, worsen drought conditions by draining local waterways, depriving vegetation, fish and other aquatic life of the water they need to survive droughts.

Filling paddling pools to cool off, taking multiple showers each day to stay clean, watering the garden to revive wilting plants – all these extra activities contribute to a sharp increase in public water use on hot and dry days. And these impacts can endure for months, as freshwater systems need a lot of additional rainfall to recover from droughts.

open image in gallery A cleaning pump can filter paddling pool water and recycle it without you needing to use more water to keep the pool clean. ( Getty/iStock )

If each person can reduce their water use during a drought, it would significantly benefit the natural world in its recovery. Here are five things you can do, starting today.

1. Shower less

Most of the water you use is in the shower. For every minute you’re under the shower head (depending on how powerful it is), around 10 litres of water drains away. Since most people shower for an average of seven minutes, half of your daily water use takes place first thing in the morning.

Turning off the shower while shampooing your hair or applying shower gel can help conserve water, as can shortening the length of your shower overall. Be sure not to switch to a bath though – the average soak in the tub uses around 80 litres of water.

open image in gallery Turning off the shower while shampooing your hair can help conserve water. ( Getty/iStock )

2. Use rainwater in the garden

A green, plastic barrel connected to a black draining pipe and stood in a garden.

During a dry spell, the average gardener can use hundreds of litres of water to keep their plants hydrated. Some people will use a watering can (good), others might leave a sprinkler on all day (bad). Most use drinking water, which is a waste – plants are happy with rain water.

Add a water butt that collects the rain which falls on your roof and use it for the garden. To find out how to install one, watch this.

3. Use the short flush

Per flush, your toilet uses about 5 litres of water, and up to 10 litres in older models. If available, use the short flush to significantly reduce how much water is wasted.

open image in gallery Use the short flush to reduce how much water is wasted. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

4. Cut back on car washing

If you need to wash your car, do it the old-fashioned way with a bucket and soap rather than hosing it down. The water contained in a bucket (roughly 30 litres) is significantly less than the average that flows through a hose (around 15 litres per minute). Better yet, avoid washing your car entirely during a drought.

5. Reuse water

If you’re washing vegetables, you could collect the water in a bowl in the sink and later give it to the plants in your house or outside. While you’re waiting for warm water to come out of a tap, use the cold to fill the kettle. Close the tap while you’re lathering your hands with soap or brushing your teeth. Though these are only small savings, they do make a difference over time.

About the author Niko Wanders is an Assistant Professor in Hydrological Extremes at Utrecht University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Inflatable pools are lovely for cooling down on the hottest days. A cleaning pump can filter the water and recycle it without you needing to use more water to keep the pool clean.

Save water, save money

All these tips can significantly reduce your water use and combat the effects of drought on the environment. They can also save you money.

If you’re able to renovate your home, it’s worth installing a system for collecting rain water which, combined with a pump, can flush toilets. In Belgium, for example, it is common practice to have such a system installed (effectively, a large underground water butt) in newly built houses.

Most people would struggle to afford these kinds of measures, and so drought-proofing homes and communities should be part of the effort to adapt countries to the extreme weather expected in a rapidly warming world.

A 16-year-old girl from Swindon has died in a “terrible accident” while on holiday in the Dominican Republic, friends of the family have said.

Abbie Lainton was on a trip to the Caribbean island during the summer holidays and awaiting her GCSE results when the fatal incident took place, according to a GoFundMe page set up by a family friend in her memory.

Two of her siblings were also said to have been “badly injured” in the accident on 30 July. The exact circumstances surrounding the incident are yet to be confirmed.

“Abbie had her whole life ahead of her,” the page’s author Becky Jamieson wrote. “She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results. She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her.”

The appeal has so far raised more than £10,000 towards an £18,000 target.

A spokesperson for the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: “Our thoughts are with the Lainton family during this difficult time.

“We are providing consular support to the family and assisting other British nationals and their families affected by the incident. We are in contact with the local authorities.”

Abbie was an avid dancer and cheerleader, with Tanwood School for Performing Arts releasing a statement calling her a “dinky dot” who “”always performed with a huge smile”.

“Abbie took her dance training and joined Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club where she once again excelled and competed all over the world,” the statement said.

“Abbie's family have been part of the Tanwood family for years, and have always offered unwavering support.We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time. You will always be in our hearts.”

Abbie was an avid dancer with an ‘infectious smile’, according to those who knew her ( GoFundMe )

Members of the Swindon Lightning Club said that Abbie was a “much-loved” member of the group.

“Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years,” a spokesperson said. “She brought so much light to our gym, and her loss has left us all heartbroken.”

Tributes poured in through the comments of statements shared on social media with one person writing that they were left “shocked to the core” by the news.

Her cheer coach Mychael James-Dixon added: “Abbie was an incredible young person, who filled every room she was in with her warmth and smile. I am still in shock and completely devastated to hear of her passing.

“In truth I’m struggling to find the words to do her justice, but I can say with 100 per cent certainty that anyone who knew her loved her and life was made that much better for having known her.”

News.content:
