On Friday, as Infantino attended the inauguration of Colombia's new president Abelardo De La Espriella, ⁠FIFA released a blistering attack on the critics of the president. It warned against what it called a "concerted and ongoing effort" to undermine Infantino, ⁠saying ⁠attempts to challenge his leadership must follow the governing ​body's statutes and democratic procedures.

FIFA also echoed the statements of several of the bodies that supported Infantino, as well as one from South American confederation ​CONMEBOL.

FIFA's statement came after reports by The ⁠Daily Telegraph about payments made by UEFA to a former employee during Infantino's time as the European governing body's general secretary, allegations he has denied and that FIFA has rejected as unfounded.

Almost 70 of FIFA's 211 member associations have said publicly they will vote for Infantino with around a dozen either withdrawing previously promised support or saying they will not vote for him.

UEFA apart, the confederations who say they have lost confidence in Infantino are not completely united, ⁠with several Asian nations backing him as ‌well as Mexico from CONCACAF.

World.title: Prison watchdog role left vacant for months, even after outgoing investigator warned of 'serious legal void'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government left the position of Canada's prison watchdog vacant for several months, despite written warnings from the outgoing correctional investigator that doing so would seriously compromise the office's powers to do its job protecting inmates.

Records obtained by CBC News under Canada's Access to Information Act reveal that former correctional investigator Ivan Zinger advised Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree that the failure to fill his position before he left "would create a serious legal void."

After around four months of sitting vacant, the role was filled by an interim investigator — a move that has itself raised concerns because of the role's temporary nature.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator (OCI) acts as an independent watchdog for prisoners across Canada, dealing with an average 4,000-5,000 complaints a year.

In previous years its work has helped trigger significant inquiries, such as the commission of inquiry into Kingston's Prison for Women in the mid-1990s that uncovered infringement of prisoners' legal rights and "cruel, inhumane and degrading" treatment of women there.

During his time as correctional investigator, Zinger flagged several problems in Canada's prisons including lack of access to adequate mental health treatment and the over-representation of Indigenous inmates.

Last year he announced he would be stepping down early from his five-year mandate.

Zinger told CBC News that he gave the government seven months' notice so it could find a new correctional investigator before he left in February.

"As my departure date came very, very close, I grew increasingly frustrated that the government had done nothing. No posting of the position, or there was no plan to replace me. So I grew concerned," he said.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree arrives at a caucus meeting on Parliament Hill in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

Warning of 'far-reaching' consequences

In a letter obtained by CBC News, dated Jan. 5, Zinger warned Anandasangaree that without a correctional investigator, the office couldn't initiate any new, non-routine investigations into problems with Canada's prison system; issue any special or annual reports; or warn prison psychologists or wardens about confidential information obtained during investigations such as suicide risks or an inmate's plans to harm other prisoners or correctional service staff.

"As these examples demonstrate, the consequences of failing to appoint either an interim or permanent CI [correctional investigator] in a timely manner would be significant and far-reaching," Zinger wrote. "In my view, ample notice was provided to allow for appropriate steps to be taken to identify a temporary or permanent successor."

In an earlier letter to Anandasangaree, dated July 16, 2025, a couple of weeks after he announced he was going to step down, Zinger said it was "critical" that his position be filled before he left.

"The role holds exclusive statutory authorities and investigative powers that cannot be delegated," he warned the minister. "As such, it is critical that the position be filled by February 2, 2026, to ensure the office remains operational, effective and compliant with its legislative mandate."

Zinger's letters provide a glimpse behind the scenes at a larger problem: delays in recent years in filling some government appointments, with some organizations being left for weeks or months without key positions being filled.

A CBC news analysis in 2023 of governor in council appointments to 206 government bodies or institutions found 416 of the 1,731 positions — almost a quarter — were either vacant or occupied by someone whose appointment had continued past its end date.

"It's administrative delays after delays. And bureaucratic inertia, if not blatant incompetence," Zinger told CBC News.

Despite Zinger's warnings, Anandasangaree has yet to name a permanent replacement.

His office says "a process to identify a full-time replacement is underway" but would not provide a timetable or say whether it will hold an open competition for the job.

Interim investigator admits there are challenges

In June, OCI executive director Valerie Phillips was named interim correctional investigator for up to one year.

In an emailed response to CBC News, Phillips said there were no delays in dealing with complaints while the investigator's position was vacant and she was granted the power to disclose information in cases where there was an imminent risk of serious harm to an inmate or correctional staff.

However, she said there were challenges dealing with Correctional Service Canada's headquarters and getting final signoffs for some reports.

Phillips said she now has the same powers as someone appointed on a longer-term basis and can initiate investigations. But she acknowledged an interim role can "create challenges when planning for longer-term strategic initiatives, implementing significant organizational change or making decisions with implications that extend beyond the interim period."

Zinger told CBC News that during the four months the position was vacant, Phillips, as executive director, didn't have the authority to do anything beyond routine processing of individual complaints.

He says he is concerned he hasn't seen any sign of a competition for the long-term job, a process he says can take five or six months.

Zinger said a key part of an ombudsman-type job like the correctional investigator is the ability to speak truth to power and not be afraid to criticize the actions — or inaction — of the government.

"If the minister goes ahead and hand-picks a person, the criticism that he may get at this point was that he [chose] somebody who will not be trying to rock the boat or would have reluctance to criticize his actions," he said.

Sen. Kim Pate is a long-time advocate for the rights of Canadian prisoners. (Ashley Burke/CBC News)

Sen. Kim Pate, a long-time advocate for prisoners' rights, said leaving the investigator's position vacant for four months is "a huge issue" and called on the government to appoint a permanent successor to Zinger.

"When you only have someone in an interim position, when they have no idea how long they'll be in that position and whether a new investigator would actually follow up on those issues, it really curtails the incentive and the ability of them to investigate issues that may very well need important and in-depth investigation," she said.

Emilie Coyle, co-executive director of the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies, which advocates for issues affecting women, girls and gender diverse people in the justice system, said the OCI is the only body with authority to enter prisons unannounced and can compel records from Correctional Service Canada.

Coyle said the absence of a correctional investigator and, consequently, "independent oversight," came as overcrowding was making conditions worse in prisons.

"It was the most critical time for people who are inside to have that independent oversight happening," she said, adding that the delay in filling the position doesn't bode well for the rights of those in prison.

NDP public safety critic Jenny Kwan says issues in Canada's prison system are 'not a priority for the government.' (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

New Democrat public safety critic Jenny Kwan said there are several issues in Canada's prison system that have to be dealt with, including the over-incarceration of Indigenous people, inadequate mental health support and barriers to rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

"I think that this is not a priority for the government," said Kwan.

Kwan said Zinger should not have had to warn Anandasangaree about the need to fill the position.

"To date, we still don't have a permanent appointment, and there is no clear process of how the government will proceed with respect to that," she said. "That should be alarming for everyone, for Canadians, for the minister who is in charge of Canada's public safety."

World.title: After Yellowknife’s only cinema closed, film fans are travelling 1,500 km to catch summer blockbusters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Over the August long weekend, Jacob Charpentier flew 1,500 kilometres from Yellowknife to Edmonton with one main mission: to see the newest blockbusters , namely Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey, on the big screen.

A self-described Marvel fan and movie-lover, Charpentier initially planned a massive weekend marathon of six or seven films — including Supergirl, Jackass, and Masters of the Universe — but limited showtimes forced him to settle on three at the Scotiabank Theatre in West Edmonton Mall: Spider-Man, The Odyssey and Minions & Monsters.

Following the permanent shutdown of Yellowknife’s Capitol Theatre earlier this year, residents in the Northwest Territories capital are experiencing their first summer in nearly eight decades without a local cinema.

“It’s kind of madness at some points thinking about it,” Charpentier says.

'It feels so isolated up here'

Charpentier, like many others in Yellowknife, has been feeling the strain of losing the local screen.

“It feels so isolated up here. The rest of the world gets to see this thing and they’re talking about it,” Charpentier said. “You can wait for streaming, but you don’t get that feeling when you’re seeing people dressed up as Spider-Man.”

Having caught every Marvel release on opening day since he was a teenager, travelling south wasn't just about screen size — it was about escaping online spoilers and sharing a cultural moment.

Jacob Charpentier as Spider-Man in 2015 (Submitted by Jacob Charpentier)

Between airfare, hotels, food and concessions, Charpentier spent roughly $1,500 for a trip that would have cost under $100 back home.

And he wasn't alone. Charpentier recognized fellow Yellowknifers in almost every concession line at the Edmonton theatre, reinforcing his belief that a cinema is a basic "staple of any town."

For 43-year-old Yellowknife resident and longtime Marvel fan Mikey McBryan, the theatre's closure and rise of streaming services means missing out on the cultural conversation entirely.

“We lost monoculture,” McBryan said. “Everybody has everything they ever wanted to watch ... It's funny enough as a 43-year-old man to say that I'm missing out because I can't see Spider-Man, but it's true.”

Yellowknife resident, Mikey McBryan and his original edition of a 1973 comic of The Amazing Spider-Man (Submitted by Mikey McBryan)

McBryan, who hasn't been able to see the film yet, notes that while Yellowknifers were previously "spoiled," they are now experiencing the same isolation smaller N.W.T. communities have faced for decades.

Both McBryan and Charpentier say they prefer supporting filmmakers legally in theatres, but acknowledge that accessibility barriers might push more Northerners toward online piracy if local options remain limited.

What’s next for Yellowknife’s screens?

McBryan says finding a viable business model remains a steep hurdle. He notes, surviving off two or three summer blockbusters a year while paying year-round overhead is a tough proposition for any operator.

“How does a full business in Yellowknife survive off maybe one or two or three big movies a year when they [have] to fill the seats every single day of the week? It's tough,” McBryan says.

Back in February, local residents met to discuss community-led solutions, but progress has stalled. According to Charpentier, building new infrastructure elsewhere is financially out of reach and the co-owners of the building that houses the former cinema , Det’on Cho Group and KingSett Capital, "haven't made it clear at all what they want to do."

Neither co-owner responded to requests for comment by publication time.

Yellowknife's Capitol Theatre in August, 2026. The old cinema closed permanently on April 1, 2026. (Saloni Bhugra/CBC)

In the meantime, grassroots groups are stepping up where they can. Cassidy Menard co-runs the Yellowknife Film Club, hosting free monthly screenings of classic movies at the Yellowknife Public Library.

She’s noticed a clear surge in audience attendance this summer.

“People say, 'You should start doing this more frequently.' Unfortunately, we just don’t have the capacity to put on more film viewings,” Menard said.

Yellowknife film club watching 1967 film, 'Network' in July 2026 (Submitted by Cassidy Menard)

While the club lacks the resources to run a commercial theatre, Menard says they would jump at the chance to collaborate with another organization if an auditorium space became available.

For now, Yellowknife’s big screen remains dark, leaving local cinephiles with few choices.

“Was it worth it? I wish it wasn’t,” Charpentier said of his $1,500 trip. “But I would pay again to do that ... I wish I could have stayed in town, though, ultimately.”

World.title: How the future of air traffic controlling could see planes directed from other cities
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Nav Canada’s Dave Sheppard saw towers popping up at airports abroad that were packed with new technology and devoid of physical staff, he had one thought: this is the future.

"When you hear the concept of the model, it seems a little bit far out there," said Sheppard, the chief technology officer for the not-for-profit corporation that oversees Canada's air traffic controllers.

"But … we looked at it and said, you know, this is a great fit for Canada.”

After years of testing cameras under intense Canadian climates, working to reassure staff of the benefits and getting the ball rolling on regulatory approvals, it seems like the future is now.

The newly completed digital aerodrome air traffic tower in Kingston, Ont., is the first of its kind in Canada.

It's topped with a camera that rotates around it, and others which can pan, tilt and zoom in on potential obstacles.

A drone image shows the digital aerodrome air traffic control tower being erected at the airport in Kingston. It's the first of its kind in Canada. (Nav Canada)

Also at the airport is a new digital control centre, where staff can advise aircraft by remotely monitoring information fed from the tower.

The next step is building a similar tower in Hamilton, to be monitored by staff about 300 kilometres away at the Kingston facility. Eventually, air traffic controllers for 10 to 15 airports could all be stationed at the eastern Ontario site.

Sheppard says the move will provide a new level of flexibility at a time of global staffing pressures, while allowing air controllers to see more than they ever have.

The union representing these workers, though, is bracing for turbulence.

Canada still 200 controllers short of target

The global shortage of air traffic controllers worsened significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic, which rocked the aviation industry.

It’s been blamed for delayed or cancelled flights.

Some have also questioned if even more serious staffing pressures in the United States have contributed to deadly incidents, like the fatal March 2026 collision involving a fire truck and an Air Canada plane at New York's LaGuardia Airport.

While Nav Canada remains about 200 people short of staffing targets, the organization says it's quickly filling the gap through a ramped-up training regime.

“This allows us to bring people in and actually recruit individuals into a location that's central where they would like to stay and live and work," Sheppard said.

It’s what Nav Canada says led them to station the pilot project in Kingston, a community he also says has a healthy pool of qualified talent.

Once it's fully set up, Nav Canada should be able to more easily fill unexpected absences that could impact service because trained backfill options are a workstation — not a city — away.

A row of 12 screens replace windows in a remote air traffic monitoring console. Controllers can control cameras to zoom in on aircraft or possible obstructions. (Nav Canada)

Union closely watching the transition

But the big idea requires buy-in from its labour force, and the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association (CATCA) has some concerns.

Union president Nick von Schoenberg called it a “significant shift,” one he feels could provide equivalent service but doesn’t seem poised to make travel safer.

The industry is facing a “demographic bubble," von Schoenberg said, with many controllers nearing the end of their careers.

Some may choose to leave the field altogether rather than uproot their families, he said.

"Even if that attrition is only ... 10 or 20 per cent, we can't afford to lose a single air traffic controller right now in Canada," von Schoenberg said.

New technology would allow air traffic controllers to see three times further than with binoculars, but the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association says seeing and hearing their surroundings helps controllers work. (Sarah Krymalowski/CBC)

Von Schoenberg also raised a raft of potential questions, both technical and on a human level.

“[This involves] replacing an existing model that has been demonstrated to work very well, and that comes at a cost — a financial and human resource cost,” he said.

“I don't think [that's] probably the wisest strategy in the near term.”

While Nav Canada has been “open and transparent” through the process, von Schoenberg said many still worry what will happen should the technology fail.

Kongsberg Geospatial president Jordan Freed, left, and Nav Canada's Dave Sheppard, right, stand in front of a console showing an infrared view of an airport. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

What is the technology like?

The new tower at Kingston is obviously different from a traditional control tower with a bulbous top ringed by windows.

Rather than sitting in the middle of things, controllers are stationed at remote workspaces behind 12 large screens positioned in a gentle curve — providing a flattened, 360-degree view.

Kongsberg Geospatial, Nav Canada’s project partner, is deploying technology already used by its parent company in Norway.

“This technology significantly improves safety from an air traffic control perspective,” argued president Jordan Freed.

New features allow controllers to toggle to an infrared view, handy during low-vision weather and at night. Moving objects are highlighted and tracked so they can zoom in to investigate.

"We're seeing the development and implementation of AI into more and more technology," said Freed.

The system "can continue to learn" as it's used, he said, becoming better at identifying aircraft, weather patterns and potential dangers.

Both Nav Canada and CATCA stress that any artificial intelligence used will leave humans firmly in the driver’s seat.

New remote monitoring stations for air traffic controllers highlight a potential danger. This recording from an airport in Norway shows a group of birds near a runway. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

The new global standard?

Experts say this move has been a long time coming and is certain to benefit the sector.

“Ten years from now, it'll be the standard,” said John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University.

The technology is much more efficient, Gradek said, and closer to what air traffic controllers already do than people might think.

“What Nav Canada is doing with this technology is adding a toolkit. It's not changing the fundamental jobs of air traffic control,” he said.

“Whether you're managing St. Thomas or London or Sarnia or Windsor from one seat, you're still managing airspace.”

Jordan Freed stands in front of a digital aerodrome air traffic control monitoring station showing a feed from a remote airport in Norway. Freed argues the technology 'improves safety from an air traffic control perspective.' (Francis Ferland/CBC)

The technology is already being used in well over a dozen nations, including at the London City Airport in the United Kingdom.



It's also in place at the Bodø Airport in Norway. Freed says the country has used this new form of remote work to expand air service to isolated areas where it’s hard to attract skilled workers.

“Now you can bring them into a larger city. You can actually have a team. There's not two people working remotely, but there's a whole team,” he said. “In fact, the first thing that strikes you when you walk into the Bodø centre is how young the team of air traffic controllers are.”

Von Schoenberg argues that this is the direction Canada should be moving in: expanding service, rather than replacing existing towers.

But with Hamilton topping the list of planned airports, the union leader says it's clear that's not on Canada's trajectory — or at least, not yet.

How to ensure it's safe

Nav Canada is right now focused on the many Canadian control towers built in the '50s, '60s and '70s that need to be replaced or significantly renovated.

Sheppard says expanding the scope of its work geographically is far in the future, but it remains a goal.

When Canada is ready to add air traffic control to areas where none exist, building a remotely monitored digital aerodrome tower will be much faster, easier and cheaper, he said.

What's mainly holding the group back is connectivity.

A traditional air traffic control tower, like this one in Ottawa, involves controllers monitoring airspace through large windows. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

To build safety and redundancy into the system, Sheppard says there should be two telecommunications service providers. That is not yet the reality in many isolated communities.

As for other failsafes, Nav Canada says the towers come with backup power and extra cameras in case one breaks or becomes obscured. Each remote-control station also has a full backup.

There’s still a lot of testing to come.

Starting this fall, a shadow team of air traffic controllers will spend a year at remote stations on site.

Once the concept has been proven safe and regulatory approvals are secured, Nav Canada will begin the transition in Hamilton.

CBC reached out to Transport Canada to find out more about the process and how it’s addressing any potential concerns about automation in the industry. It did not provide a response by deadline.

World.title: Canada’s ‘suicidal empathy’ hits its terminal stage: Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

Civilizations die from suicide, not murder, as a famous historian once said. And Canada is in the process of administering MAID to itself, says author and professor Gad Saad. He discusses his new bestselling book, “Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind,” with Brian Lilley. And he explains the fatal flaw of excessive empathy — and how Canada is rapidly succumbing to it. Radical values imposed by our institutions, embodied in the extreme by the last prime minister, frame our history as shameful. They have led us to embrace immigrants who reject us. And they have made us tolerate the intolerant. It’s why Saad says he’s moving out of Canada, although he explains how our government isn’t making it easy for him to leave. World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky

The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance.
