World.title: Why Poland’s right-wing split may not save Donald Tusk
World.content:
However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right.

PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month, when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies.

The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious.

Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support.

“Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week.

He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future.

World.title: A new rival is forcing Italy’s Meloni back to her far-right roots
World.content:
While France and other countries tightened border checks, Italy went further and announced it had suspended the EU’s free-movement Schengen agreement with Madrid. Now, in Italian airports, passengers from Spain are asked to join a different line.

Meloni’s office has made clear it has no intention of lifting the controls until at least Aug. 15, escalating the clash with Spain, which retaliated by imposing checks on travelers from Italy.

“We will not back down one millimeter on illegal immigration,” Meloni posted on X while her allies attacked the socialist Spanish government, accusing it of failing to manage migration flows. “Defending our borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriation will continue to be this government’s policy,” she added.

The clash with Spain is just the latest sign that the Italian leader is doing all she can to secure her core, hard-right electorate in the face of a challenge from the right by Roberto Vannacci, a former general and member of the European Parliament.

With an election expected as early as next spring, Vannacci’s far-right National Future party has been advancing in the polls, overtaking one of Meloni’s coalition partners, the far-right League party, and gaining on another, Forza Italia, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

For Meloni, who began her political career in the youth wing of Italy’s post-fascist movement, the challenge strikes particularly close to home.

World.title: Firefighters struggle to put out three wildfires in southwestern Spain
World.content:
Firefighters struggled on Monday to control three large wildfires in southern Spain that has forced the evacuation of around 800 people due to shifting winds and difficult terrain, officials said.

 

More than 600 firefighters backed by 26 water-dropping aircraft were battling the blaze which broke out last week in the Andalusian province of Huelva, said the region's minister for emergencies, Antonio Sanz.

"We are facing an extremely difficult, complex and dangerous wildfire, with the weather conditions continuing to offer us no respite. It is a long-distance race full of obstacles," he said.

"We have to be realistic: there is no forecast that the fire will be brought under control any time soon. There are still hours and probably days of intense work ahead."

Crews worked through the night, carrying out controlled burns and creating mechanised firebreaks, but authorities said rugged terrain and weather conditions had slowed progress.

A house and belongings destroyed by a wildfire are photographed as the fire continues to spread near Pelayos de la Presa, 28 July, 2026 AP Photo

More than 20,000 hectares of land are currently enclosed by the fire, but authorities stressed this figure refers to the area contained within the fire line and does not mean all of it has burned.

Officials on Monday ordered the evacuation of the municipality of El Madrono, which has a population of around 300 people, bringing to about 800 the total number of evacuees.

Crews are also battling blazes in Castellón and Segovia. All three fires have been graded level two for severity.

Spain is enduring a tough summer for wildfires, with around three dozen blazes having forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, especially in the centre of the country.

One that raged in July in the Avila region near Madrid was considered the biggest Spain had seen in recent history, laying waste to some 50,000 hectares.

Early in July, another sweeping blaze caused 14 deaths in Almeria province in Andalusia.

Europe has suffered a succession of heatwaves and droughts this year, which scientists say have been aggravated by human-generated climate change.

World.title: EU stands in 'solidarity' with Euronews following ban in Belarus
World.content:
The European Union has condemned Belarus’ decision to designate Euronews as an “extremist” media organisation, saying it forms part of a "broader pattern of repression targeting independent media."

 

“It is an ongoing effort to restrict freedom of the press,” said Anitta Hipper, the EU’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and security.

“The EU shares its solidarity with Euronews.”

The comments follow a wave of support for Euronews following last week's listing from Minsk, including from Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya who described the move as a “shameful” attempt to curb press freedom.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola posted on social media platform X that Europe continues to stand with the people of Belarus, and will continue advocating for a country where liberty, media freedom and the will of its people prevail.

“Six years after people stood up for a new future, their voices have not been silenced,” she said, according to the online statement.

“Belarus will be free.”

According to Belarus-based media, the Belarusian information ministry last week placed Euronews’ website on its "Republican List of Extremist Materials”. The ruling is subject to immediate execution under Belarusian civil procedure rules.

The decision means access to the Euronews website will now be restricted in the landlocked Eastern European country, while readers could face administrative penalties for storing or distributing its content.

The broadcaster said the designation risks criminalising its audience as well as limiting access to its factual journalism.

‘Badge of honour’

European Federation of Journalists President Maja Sever said on Monday the “extremist” designation is an attempt to discredit and intimidate independent media, and follows the Kremlin’s example.

“This baseless accusation should be seen as a badge of honour: the so-called ‘extremist’ media are in fact those that defend the Belarusian people’s right to access free, pluralistic and independent information,” she said.

The definition of "extremism" in Russia is open to interpretation, and it enables the authorities to target minorities, political opposition, or stifle freedom of expression or assembly.

Russian President Vladimir Putin right greets Belarusian President Aliaksandr Lukashenka during their meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia, 26 September, 2025. AP

Martin Roux from Reporters Without Borders’ (RSF) crisis desk said Belarus is following Russia’s example by utilising anti-terrorism legislation to criminalise journalism.

“This defamatory label targets foreign media, including Euronews and, previously, the Polish Press Agency, that worry the regime because they cover a country closed off to any information sources contradicting the official narrative, and where 20 media professionals remain in detention,” he said.

Since 2020, RSF has identified more than 60 media outlets designated as “extremist”. In Russia, this includes Euronews, France 24 and the BBC.

There are up to 48 journalists and media professionals imprisoned in Russia, the RFS states, with up to 21 media workers currently imprisoned in Belarus and many more living in exile, according to the Association of Belarusian Journalists (BAJ).

‘A brutal campaign against all dissent’

The comments come a day after the sixth anniversary of the 2020 presidential elections in Belarus.

The vote was widely seen as fraudulent by the EU and many Western governments, as well as opposition figures and citizens. In the days following, protesters took to the streets to contest the official results, which handed Aliaksandr Lukashenka another term in power.

Demonstrations were met with a sweeping crackdown, including violent arrests and the detention of thousands of people.

Police officers kick a demonstrator during a mass protest following presidential election in Minsk, Belarus, on 10 August, 2020. AP

Amnesty International describe Lukashenka’s contested win as one that occurred in a context of “total fear and repression” — which has only heightened.

“Ever since the 2020 presidential election, the already profound human rights crisis in Belarus has deepened even further,” said Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director.

“Through a brutal campaign against all dissent, the authorities have created a suffocating climate of fear, silencing anything and anyone who challenges the government.”

Despite the release of several political prisoners over the past year, the EU's foreign policy arm, the European External Action Service (EEAS), estimates 800 individuals remain arbitrarily detained, with many subjected to ill-treatment, torture, and no access to essential health services.

Belarusian human rights organisation Viasna says the list of people it recognises as political prisoners grows weekly.

World.title: Danube water level rising: Another Paks nuclear plant turbine may restart
World.content:
The phased reactivation of the previously shut-down capacity has begun at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, after the level of the River Danube started to rise.

 

Once the river had climbed back above the critical low recorded a week earlier, it became possible for one turbine to start producing electricity again from Monday evening. The reconnection is taking place under strict technical and safety conditions.

At the beginning of August, the Danube’s water level dropped to a historic low, reaching minus 134 centimetres at Paks. As a result, three of the four reactor units had to be shut down gradually and in a controlled manner. Only a single turbine remained in operation.

Thanks to rainfall over the Austrian catchment areas, the river began to swell along its upper reaches. That flood wave has now reached the Paks section as well. A rise of 19 centimetres in the water level provides enough volume to extend safe cooling.

The MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant in Paks, 29 July, 2026 MTVA - Media Service Support and Asset Management Fund

Plant increases power output

With the launch of another generating unit, the plant’s output to the grid will increase from the 240 megawatts recorded during the critical period to 500 megawatts.

During the restart and operation of the nuclear power plant, nuclear safety takes absolute precedence over electricity production, so the reconnection has to meet several stringent requirements. In terms of adequate pump pressure, the rise in the Danube has restored the efficiency of the cold-water channel pumps, ensuring that the condensers can be cooled.

The systems responsible for cooling the reactor core and the spent fuel pools must function flawlessly; they remained continuously in operation even during the period of low water. Before the turbine can be started, an adequate vacuum has to be created in the condenser. The quality of the secondary-circuit water also needs to be checked.

The reactor’s thermal output and the volume of steam are not adjusted in one go but synchronised step by step with the generator’s connection to the grid, according to a strict timetable.

Around half a million components also have to be subjected to diagnostics. Operating specialists will ensure that the heat and the temporary shutdown have not caused microscopic material defects in the equipment.

World.title: Russia plans to fire 200 ballistic missiles at once, Ukraine's drone commander says
World.content:
Russia's military can currently fire a simultaneous salvo of 77 ballistic missiles and plans to increase that number to 200, according to Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, the officer leading Ukraine's drone forces.

 

"Even if they only manage half of that, it will all be flying at us," he told the Associated Press news agency on Monday.

The warning points to one of Ukraine's most exposed vulnerabilities - a shortage of interceptors for the US-made Patriot systems, the only weapon in Kyiv’s arsenal capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.

That shortfall means dozens of missiles fired during mass barrages already get through and hit their targets. And while the there have been mixed signals form the US regarding a possible licence for Patriot interceptor missiles, Ukrainian forces have to look for other solutions.

Brovdi said the only way to bring the number down is to strike every facility involved in producing them, the logic behind Ukraine’s log-range strikes deep into Russia’s territory.

Emergency services personnel work to extinguish a fire of residential buildings following a Russian missiles attack in Odesa, 9 August, 2026 Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP/Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP

Ukraine’s campaign in Crimea

Brovdi's warning came amid Ukraine’s campaign of cutting Crimea of Russian control and ground lines of communication.

He said his units could strike seven times as many targets on the peninsula if Western funding, already pledged, arrived faster.

As it stands, he put his forces' equipment at just 14% of what full capacity would require.

"It's not that the production capacity of Ukrainian manufacturers doesn't allow us to make the necessary quantities," he said. "It's the banal problem of untimely financing, which our partners do allocate, but which moves significantly slower than our plans."

Since the offensive began in late June, Ukrainian forces have hit rail bridges, oil depots and power infrastructure, disrupting supply lines and destroying more than 300 Russian air defence assets - surface-to-air systems, radar stations and electronic warfare equipment - to clear a path for drones.

Rescue workers try to put out a fire of a residential building and cars burning after a Russian air guided bomb strike in Zaporizhzhia, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Brovdi said Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russian authorities had since ordered military commands and security services off the peninsula, along with a covert order to remove secret archives and artworks.

Moscow is meanwhile working to close the gap.

Brovdi said Russia is deploying jamming systems that will partly degrade Starlink connectivity in Crimea and is building its own satellite communication network, which, Brovdi said is "a risk for the entire planet," he said, "because a dictatorship will gain access to information across the whole globe."

World.title: Inside the Italian prison where inmates find freedom through theatre
World.content:
For some prisoners in Italy, life behind bars has become an unlikely route towards freedom.

 

At Volterra prison, one of Italy’s oldest jails, professional theatre-makers have spent almost four decades working alongside inmates to create ambitious performances that challenge conventional ideas about punishment, rehabilitation and the role of art.

The project, known as the “Compagnia della Fortezza”, was founded by director Armando Punzo, who originally entered the prison looking for actors for a theatre company unlike any other.

"I wanted to put theatre to the test in a situation where, even if naively, I thought, and I believe it was the case, that art and culture had absolutely nothing to do with it. And I found that extremely interesting and challenging,” says Punzo.

Instead of professional actors, he found a multicultural group of prisoners with little or no connection to theatre.

"I encountered people who had never once reflected on themselves differently. They were deeply immersed, just as we all are, in their ordinary lives, their lives were vastly different from ours, yet driven by the exact same mechanism,” he says.

"Being immersed in one’s ordinary life, a life that was evidently extremely difficult, both for themselves and for others. Yet, I also found people capable of reflecting on themselves. This tells us that art and culture can truly reach everyone; if they fail to do so, it is simply because the necessary work to make that happen has not been done," he adds.

A new production is created each year, while previous performances are revisited and brought back to the stage as part of a continuous process of research and artistic development.

Prisoners are involved in the creative process itself, working alongside professional theatre-makers across different aspects of the productions.

Finding freedom in confinement

For many, it has become an important part of their lives and an opportunity to engage with a form of expression they had never previously considered.

Giacomo arrived in Volterra from another prison in 2024. He had requested a transfer to this facility specifically because he was aware of the theatre work being done here, and he was immediately integrated into the company.

"Life on the outside leads you to lose yourself, and to lose all those aspects that, however silly it may sound to say, I am actually rediscovering in here. The metaphor, which I find incredibly important, is that by losing my freedom in here, within a state of total confinement, I am finding total openness,” he shares.

That same openness allows prisoners to work side-by-side with other theatre professionals every day to create the shows.

"Theatre can transform any space. Doing so is inherent to the language of theatre, and therefore, this is theatre. When we do this, the prison steps aside, much like an actor who sets aside a part of himself when stepping onto the stage,” says Viola Ferro, a young actress that chose to join the acting company.

Rehabilitation beyond punishment

For prison director Valentina Bruno, the theatre project forms part of a wider approach to rehabilitation, in which prisoners are treated as people rather than simply as inmates.

"They (prisoners) feel that the staff cares for them in the best possible way. They feel valued as individuals, not merely as numbers or files. They feel that they matter, and that their family context matters too, given the frequent contact we maintain with their relatives”, she says.

“Above all, I believe what they strongly feel is hope: the hope of returning to society, whether upon completing their sentence or even sooner, as changed individuals capable of giving something back to the community,” she adds.

The work of the company is perhaps most striking when its performances open the prison to the outside world. The courtyard becomes a theatre, with the fortress walls forming the backdrop and members of the public entering the prison to watch the performances.

Writer Maria Nadotti, who regularly attends the performances, says the company represents something increasingly unusual in contemporary theatre.

"I have absolute admiration for the work of the “Compagnia della Fortezza” and for something that, in my view, is increasingly rare in theatre, and not just in Italy, a combination of imagination, joy, energy, and an absolute passion for wonder, wonder is the soul of the world, and it is all present here,” she says.

World.title: Record 230 migrants cross English Channel in single small boat, French officials say
World.content:
A record 230 migrants in one small boat crossed the English Channel to Britain, France's lifeboat service and UK media said on Monday, in the latest example of larger numbers of people packing into a single vessel.

 

The 230, including more than 20 children, were counted aboard the rubber dinghy as it departed the northeastern French coast amid chaotic scenes late Sunday, the SNSM lifeboat service said in a statement posted online.

The number breaks the previous record for a single boat, set last month when 165 people successfully crossed the busy shipping waterway.

The SNSM said on Monday it was "a new and sad record for the number of people crammed onto these flimsy boats."

A UK-bound dinghy carrying more than 150 people capsized in the Channel last week after its engine caught fire, prompting a major search-and-rescue operation.

In the latest record-breaking journey, French lifeboats escorted the dinghy up to British waters, before being relieved by the British, Jean-Marc Lamblin, the SNSM's local branch director, told the AFP news agency.

A general view of small boats and inflatable dinghies in a Border Force compound in Dover, 26 February, 2025 AP/Copyright 2025 The AP. All rights reserved

He noted the rubber dinghy was around 15 metres long.

"For the past three months, we've been seeing more and more" of these 15-metre dinghies, Lamblin added.

"We recently passed the record of 150 people; we didn't think there could be more, but now there really are no limits anymore."

The UK interior ministry, which did not confirm the exact number aboard the boat, condemned the "the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson said it was "shocking" to see "appalling images ... of young babies being put into these unseaworthy craft."

"They show the reality behind the ruthless smuggling gangs that are prepared to risk human lives for profit," he added.

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a visit to HM Coastguard Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Dover, 1 August, 2026 AP Photo

Britain has been grappling with how to curb the perilous and politically contentious crossings, which in recent years have seen tens of thousands of migrants arriving annually on the shores of southeast England.

Since taking power in 2024, centre-left Labour has sought to "smash the gangs" facilitating the journeys, including through increased cooperation with France.

In April, London signed a new three-year deal with Paris over the crossings, agreeing to pay up to €766 million to boost French law enforcement.

The UK government argues the strategy is working, noting year-on-year migrant small boat arrivals in the first half of 2026 were down more than 42% to just over 14,000 people.

However, recent weeks have seen a spike, with a daily record for the year set on 29 July when 752 people crossed.

World.title: Now open: A gorgeous new resort overlooking the waterways of Hoi An
World.content:
Hoi An, with its UNESCO-listed Ancient Town, is on most travellers' first-time itineraries to Vietnam.

 

And, if you’re planning a visit to the former trading port and need somewhere to stay, you might just want to take a look at NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An, Tapestry Collection by Hilton.

Newly opened at the start of August, the property is found along the Co Co river in Cam Thanh village, which is best known for its basket boat rides.

The gorgeous resort was designed by Vietnamese architect Vo Trong Nghia, with biophilic architecture that’s meant to create an open-air sanctuary that blends with its surroundings.

“Tapestry Collection by Hilton is a collection of independent boutique hotels, each woven with an original, vibrant story shaped by its locale,” Alexander Shockley, lifestyle and collection brands at Hilton in Asia Pacific, said.

“NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An is a compelling expression of what makes this brand resonate globally – uplifting design, food and beverage grounded in place, and experiences that invite local exploration and adventure. As we introduce the Tapestry Collection to Vietnam, this property brings the soul of Hoi An to life in a way that feels fresh, authentic, and distinctly its own.”

What to expect at NHAAN Resort & Spa

The 174-key property offers a number of room categories, including some with direct pool access.

As you may have guessed from the name, one of the highlights of the resort will be the spa, which is set to open later this month.

The eforea spa & health club is located on the hotel’s rooftop and offers views over the waterscape. The wellbeing offering also spans a 24-hour gym, and outdoor infinity pool and a yoga deck.

Plenty of tourists head to Vietnam purely for its food, and you can explore the region’s cuisine through the hotel’s four restaurants and bars.

At Plait Restaurant, guests can dine on locally caught seafood prepared over an open Korean grill, while Keng Restaurants serves Vietnamese specialties all day.

Bong Lounge, which has a design inspired by the 500-year craft legacy of nearby Kim Bong Carpentry Village, is the place to be for coconut cocktails.

For those who want to spend their days soaking up rays in the pool, you can grab poolside bites and drinks at Nipa Pool Bar.

On the flip side, guests are just a 10-minute drive from Hoi An Ancient Town, and you can also book in for pottery-throwing, woodcarving and lantern-making workshops through the hotel if you’re looking for cultural immersion.

World.title: Saudi factory fire kills 16 Bangladeshis, Dhaka announces
World.content:
Bangladesh's foreign ministry said it was in "deep shock" on Monday, after reporting the deaths of 16 citizens in a sofa factory fire in Saudi Arabia the previous day.

 

Dhaka's Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said that there was "constant communication" with local authorities through the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia.

"Officials have been instructed to ensure the speedy repatriation of the bodies of the deceased expatriates and to secure all necessary government assistance and compensation for their families," he added.

Around seven million Bangladeshis work overseas — the majority in the Middle East.

The civil defence agency in the Saudi capital said a fire at an unlicensed facility where furniture was upholstered had been extinguished, without providing details about any casualties.

Photo of the 16 Bangladesh nationals released by the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment. Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment

"Riyadh civil defence put out a fire at an unlicensed site being used for furniture upholstery," the agency said in a post on X.

"The necessary regulatory procedures were subsequently completed regarding the site."

Like many Gulf nations, Saudi Arabia relies on a vast number of labourers from the subcontinent to help bolster its workforce, especially with jobs involving manual labour.

Reports in Saudi media estimate that over three million Bangladeshi nationals reside in the kingdom.

Foreign workers in Saudi Arabia do everything from management to cleaning the streets and waiting on tables, in a society where many citizens are reluctant to take jobs they consider menial.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?
World.content:
Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The so-called "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" between the three Sunni Muslim-majority states is meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty and threats from the Iran war.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The alliance has been likened to a NATO-style alliance and on Friday, the Pakistani foreign ministry said that an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all.

But experts and analysts have been quick to point out that the deal is unlikely to work that way — at least at first.

On Saturday, Yemen's Houthi group targeted Saudi Arabian oil facilities in Jizan. A July attack on the same facility is seen here Image: Social Media/REUTERS

For example, on the weekend the Houthi rebel group in Yemen fired at Saudi Arabian oil facilities again. The Houthis consider Saudi Arabia their enemy and are also aligned with Iran. The latter has also targeted Saudi Arabia after the US and Israel attacked it, starting a war in late February, because it sees the Saudis as a US ally.

But following the Houthi attack on the weekend, neither Turkey nor Pakistan sprang to the Saudis' defense. Nor are they likely to attack Iran, analysts say. In fact, Pakistan is acting as a mediator between Iran and the US currently.

Mecca agreement an 'elastic defense pact'

This arrangement is meant as more of a deterrent and as an "elastic defense pact," Dania Thafer, executive director of the Washington-based think tank the Gulf International Forum, or GIF, told DW late last week.

"If you look at the parties in this agreement, you have Saudi Arabia, which is in the middle of this conflict. But you also have Turkey and Pakistan, who both have relations with Iran and both have relations with the US. So I think it's an extra layer of deterrence, if you will, for Saudi Arabia," Thafer explained. "I think Saudi Arabia is looking at a layered deterrence approach to regional threats as they emerge."

This new alliance is likely to work out in various stages with the short-term goal being a "stabilized region," Kamran Bokhari, a senior fellow at the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told DW.

Technology transfer and investment

Longer term goals will involve defense cooperation rather than fighting, other experts have said.

"The three countries complement each other unusually well," Andreas Krieg, a lecturer in security at King's College London, told news agency Agence France-Presse last week.

Saudi Arabia has oil wealth but limited defense technology and has been reliant on the US up until now. Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan need investment and have strong armed forces, and in Turkey's case an advanced defense-industrial sector, Krieg explained. Pakistan is the only one with nuclear weapons of the three.

"Turkey has technology and production capacity but needs markets and investment. Pakistan has a workforce, military institutions and nuclear deterrent, but needs financing and industrial capabilities," Krieg noted.

Who does the Mecca pact target?

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on. Egypt is thought to be a potential partner but also has other allies to consider, including the United Arab Emirates. The latter have not joined and relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia are currently strained.

The Turkish official also said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

Yet there's no doubt the agreement has been understood as a deterrent, mainly against two other nations, Iran and Israel.

The Mecca pact's objectives are not about some kind of military victory, Khalid al-Jaber, director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs wrote in a Sunday op-ed for Qatari news outlet, Al Jazeera . "It is the prevention of hegemony."

"Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran," he continued. "The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region."

Damage in Iran: The country was attacked by the US and Israel in late February and the war is ongoing, although peace talks also continue Image: Morteza Akhoondi/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

How does Israel feel about it?

Two of the signatories to the agreement — Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — don't recognize Israel and have no official relations with it, even though at least in Saudi Arabia's case there are likely some covert ties. Turkey does recognize Israel but the relationship is strained at the moment, due to Israel's activity in Gaza that Turkey has called genocide.

Turkish leader Erdogan said last week that Israel's actions in Syria and Lebanon also constitute a threat to Turkish security.

"The development [of the Mecca pact] poses significant challenges for Israel, pushes the prospect of normalization with Riyadh further out of reach and cuts short the vision of a 'new Middle East'," Oshrit Birvadker, a research fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, wrote in a Saturday editorial for the outlet Israel Hayom .

Birvadker also believes that the new trilateral alliance will increase the growing rivalry and tensions between Turkey and Israel.

Mixed reactions in Iran

The Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University looked at how the Iranians were reacting.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not seem too upset by the agreement. On the social media platform, X (formerly Twitter) he posted that "when Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on."

Observers took this to be a positive, part of Iran's argument for pushing the US out of the region.

Some Iranian observers thought that the Saudis might be trying to leverage the better relations that the Turkish and Pakistanis have with the Iranians, to make itself safer from Iranian attacks. But other Iranian politicians were more critical, saying that Saudi Arabia wasn't safe with the US as an ally and wouldn't be safe with Turkey and Pakistan either.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Large earthquake hits western Colombia causing damage
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, initially measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia. Tremors were also felt in neighboring Ecuador, as well as in Panama and Venezuela.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning, with reports of the tremors being felt in the capital Bogota and even far south across the border in Quito in Ecuador.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

What did officials say as first responses?

"We have just experienced a severe seismic event in the department of Choco. We are concerned about aftershocks," the governor of the Choco region, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said online.

"Although the epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, in the capital Quibdo there are injuries and severe damage to buildings. We are already conducting the damage assessment to issue the first official report," Cordoba-Curi said. Quibdo is home to around 150,000 people.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) initially measured the quake at magnitude 7.4, although Colombia's national authority logged a smaller figure.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

Bogota residents evacuated city-center buildings as a precaution on Monday Image: Ivan Valencia/AP Photo/picture alliance

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

World.title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
World.content:
Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.

For decades, global efforts towards the eradication of malaria, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have focused essentially on West and Central Africa where the disease is most endemic.

The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region.

To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa. It's transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

The WHO warned in April 2025 that recent funding cuts were jeopardising malaria control efforts, with more than half of malaria-endemic countries surveyed reporting moderate or severe disruptions to malaria services.

A study published in The Lancet found that the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine reduced all-cause mortality among vaccine-eligible children by 13.2% in pilot programmes in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.

A changing disease landscape

Malaria transmission is most efficient within temperature ranges common across many tropical regions of West and Central Africa, according to a new study by nature .

Tanzania's bold experiment against malaria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Malaria transmission by mosquitoes usually peaks at temperatures of around 25 degrees Celsius (77 Fehrenheit) and becomes much less likely when temperatures drop below 16 degrees or rise above 34 degrees Celsius, largely because the malaria parasite must complete part of its life cycle inside the mosquito, a process that is highly temperature-dependent..

Because of this, malaria transmission has historically been most favourable across many tropical parts of West and Central Africa, where temperatures frequently fall within the range most suitable for transmission.

In contrast, some parts of Southern Africa and the highlands of East Africa have historically remained cool enough to keep the spread of malaria at bay, preventing the disease from becoming a major public health burden.

That, however, is beginning to change. The nature study found that rising temperatures are making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for malaria transmission, while parts of West Africa are becoming too hot for optimal transmission.

What does this mean for the continent?

Climate change is not only heating up the continent, it's redistributing risks, says Olugbenga Mokuolu, Professor of Paediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.

Although West African countries like Nigeria fall under areas that are "too hot for malaria to thrive, this is not good news to celebrate either, because a world that's too hot for malaria is not a good world for children's health overall," Mokuolu, who also serves as an advisor to the Nigerian Minister of Health on malaria elimination, told DW.

"The same heat that's inconvenient for mosquitoes is dangerous for people," he added, noting that climate is "not the primary driving factor of malaria, funding, drug/insecticide resistance, and health system strength still matter more."

Olugbenga continued that the elimination and prevention of malaria on the continent could become "a story of two very different regions: West/Central Africa may get a small, unplanned assist from climate, while East and southern Africa, historically lower-burden areas, face a growing new threat that could undo hard-won gains."

Are African health systems keeping pace?

Climate change is fundamentally changing the geography of disease on the continent, Olumide Idowu, founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, told DW.

Malaria research in Germany targets parasite’s life cycle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Idowu added that many African countries have developed adaptation plans but implementation has lagged behind the pace of climate change.

Although Africa is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, it remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change — posing systemic threats to the economy, infrastructure, and even its fragile health systems.

Idowu mentioned that without a significant increase in "investment at home, reinforcement of local institutional capacity and embedding health as a core pillar of climate resilience, many African countries risk being unprepared for the changing epidemiological landscape that climate change is creating."

The regions expected to be hardest hit are also regions less accustomed to fighting malaria today, the study revealed.

"Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to this evolving threat, including getting ready now to run more aggressive anti-malaria programmes in cooler areas where risk is rising," Olugbenga said.

He also urged countries in West and Central Africa to sustain malaria elimination efforts, warning that resistance to insecticides and drugs, funding gaps and weak health systems could easily negate any reduction in malaria transmission associated with rising temperatures.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Middle East: Iran wants US concessions before opening Hormuz
World.content:
Skip next section Iran demands concessions from US before reopening Strait of Hormuz

08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Iran demands concessions from US before reopening Strait of Hormuz

An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States met its conditions.

"It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions," Esmail Baghaei said Monday.

What are Iran's demands on the US?

In a statement over the weekend, a member of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and Revolutionary Guards commander said Tehran had the following demands of the US:

Never to threaten Iran again

Pay compensation for months of war damage

Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip

Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area

Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets

The impasse over the Strait of Hormuz has led to a global jump in fuel prices.

Iran is holding talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including a possible temporary shipping corridor, but it has said any actual reopening depends on negotiations with the United States.

On Sunday, however, US President Donald Trump said the US not engaged in major talks with Iran.

"We are low-keying it," he said, according to US media outlet Axios. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."

Trump also expressed his optimism that a satisfactory conclusion would eventually be reached.

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he said of the war.

World.title: ASEAN closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
World.content:
Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.

For years, governments across Southeast Asia largely approached the region's online fraudsters as a matter for the police, anti-trafficking agencies and border authorities.

But these bodies have appearently failed to stem the rise of international cyberscam cartels. The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes, with some of its centers operating under the protection of armed or politically connected groups.

Now, ASEAN governments seem increasingly willing to tackle the threat as a united bloc.

Myanmar approves death penalty for cyberscam bosses

Signs of this shift were visible at the controversial meeting in Bangkok on August 6 between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Min Aung Hlaing, the head of Myanmar's military government.

The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centres along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.

Thailand also offered support for Myanmar's participation in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial-intelligence bodies. Myanmar's military-backed parliament had already voted in favour of applying the death penalty on those caught operating online scam centres.

Dream job abroad? It could be a trafficking trap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While visiting Cambodia late last month, Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Arif Havas Oegroseno also proposed a joint task force to combat online scam syndicates.

And last week, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Thai Prime Minister Charnvirakul held talks in Jakarta where they agreed their two countries must lead the way and strengthen ASEAN's resilience against scam groups.

Online scams grew into an 'economic security threat'

A UN estimate published last month put the annual losses from cyber scammers — many of whom are located in Southeast Asia — at between $88.3 and $114.1 (between €76 billion and €98 billion) globally in 2025.

Artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies, encrypted communications and deepfake technology have made their operations cheaper and harder to detect.

Criminals in Southeast Asia increasingly use recruiters, money launderers, and brokers to target victims across the world [FILE: March 2026] Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

"Cyber scams in Southeast Asia have evolved beyond a conventional cybercrime issue and should be viewed as an economic security threat," Hai Luong, a lecturer at Australia's Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, told DW.

Impact of cybercrime felt around the world

Governments in Southeast Asia have already had to respond to pressure from the US, the EU and China as their online cartels drew international attention.

In October 2025, the US designated Cambodia's Prince Group, one of the country's largest conglomerates, as a transnational criminal organisation and imposed sanctions on 146 people and companies connected to it.

US authorities also charged Chinese-born Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies. Cambodia eventually revoked Chen's citizenship and extradited him to China.

Chinese-born Chen Zhi, believed to be one of the top bosses of Cambodia's scam industry, was extradited to China Image: China's Ministry of Public Security/AFP

Prince Group's business empire extended across real estate, finance and other sectors in Cambodia. US authorities allege that criminal revenues were mixed with legitimate commercial activities through an international network of companies.

Washington has also sanctioned other Southeast Asian individuals and companies accused of investing in scam compounds and laundering money.

The EU followed last month, imposing sanctions on Prince Group and Jin Bei Group in Cambodia and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army in Myanmafor alleged involvement in cyberscams.

Cambodia moves against US-sanctioned banks

In 2024, the United States Institute of Peace estimated that Cambodia's cyber-scam industry generated more than $12.5 billion annually, equivalent to roughly a third of the country's formal economy.

The collapse of several scam-linked conglomerates has raised concerns about how the economic shockwaves will affect the rest of the country. At the same time, other voices say negative publicity around scamming is hurting the country's tourism sector and keeping away foreign investors.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has acknowledged that the illicit scam economy is damaging legitimate businesses and has vowed a systematic crackdown on online scam networks, including greater scrutiny of the financial sector.

Inside Cambodia's scam industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The National Bank of Cambodia has shuttered at least six financial institutions since the start of the year. Three commercial banks whose licences were revoked in August had all been sanctioned by the US over alleged links to scam networks.

On August 4, the Singaporean government introduced legislation that would expand information-sharing between police and service providers, allow authorities to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and strengthen restrictions on financial, telecommunications and online services supplied to suspected offenders.

Criminal groups capitalize on government inefficiencies

As ASEAN nations try to clamp down on cybercriminals, the region's greatest weakness is its fragmentation, Sophal Ear, an associate professor at Arizona State University's Thunderbird School of Global Management, told DW.

"Criminal organizations operate seamlessly across borders while governments continue responding through separate agencies with different mandates and limited coordination," he said.

Ear added that the financial infrastructure used to move and conceal criminal proceeds can often prove more resilient than the law-enforcement architecture designed to dismantle it.

What is in ASEAN's anti-crime plan?

Now, the regional governments seem to be catching on — at least judging by ASEAN's new Plan of Action in Combating Transnational Crime for 2026–2035.

The plan calls for improved intelligence-sharing between national law-enforcement agencies and financial-intelligence units, joint investigations, better cross-border coordination and stronger capacity among anti-money-laundering regulators.

ASEAN has also recently established a joint working group to combat money laundering.

But ASEAN's consensus-based system still heavily relies on national governments implementing those commitments and sharing sensitive financial and law-enforcement information.

"In practice, governments should prioritise disrupting the financial infrastructure, labour supply chains, technological services, and transnational business models that sustain scam operations rather than focusing solely on individual offenders," said Luong from Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Moving beyond money mules

Asha Hemrajani, senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, agreed that the region needs to take a "holistic, not siloed" approach to attack the entire cyberscam business model.

Scam factory: Behind Asia's cyber slavery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The shared objective should be to identify and dismantle crime syndicate leadership, financial networks and enabling infrastructure, not just arrest money mules or raid individual scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar," Hemrajani said.

This includes official scrutiny of high-risk corporate structures and checking sources of funding, as well as a much tougher stance against money laundering, she added. Hemrajani also recommended ASEAN sanctioning business groups linked to the cyberscam networks, similar to how Washington cut off sanctioned Southeast Asian companies from the entire US economy.

Criminal groups have largely survived previous crackdowns by simply moving workers, technology and money to new places and new compounds. In order to fight the online cartels, ASEAN should do more than just closing scam centres. The real challenge is making the regional economy itself harder for them to exploit.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: India: Student anger over alleged exam issues spreads to Jharkhand
World.content:
Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.

Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process.

Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly.

The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters.

The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi.

Protesters clashed with police Monday as they marched towards the state parliament Image: ANI Video Grab

In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led "Cockroach" protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike.

Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated.

"The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW.

He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned.

But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs.

At least six protesters are on hunger strike in Jharkhand Image: ANI News/IMAGO

What sparked the protests in Jharkhand?

The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July.

Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated.

Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure.

But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem.

Devendra Nath Mahto has been on hunger strike for nine days and has lost more than 10 kilograms [FILE: August 4, 2026] Image: Somnath Sen/ANI

What are the protesters' demands?

The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated.

They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery.

The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies.

The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken.

"The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW.

Anger at civil service recruitment exams in Jharkhand has been simmering for years Image: ANI Photo

Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India?

The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers.

That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan .

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters.

But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined.

Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi.

"Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system," Bora told DW.

"They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future."

Student leader Neha Bora (wearing glasses) joined the protesters in Ranchi Image: Yousuf Sarfaraz/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights.

Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition.

"Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW.

"The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added.

Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12.

"The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment.

India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government

The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media, hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession.

The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission.

But India's youth are refusing to stop there.

Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure.

For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest.

"We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW.

World.title: UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino
World.content:
A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.

Gianni Infantino's already perilous position as FIFA president took another blow on Monday, as three continental football federations banded together in an apparent attempt to try to force him out.

An "Open Letter to the Football Family" signed by the heads of UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia) appeared to take aim at Infantino — without actually mentioning him by name.

"This is about something more fundamental: the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it. Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding — or demanding — power to be held," the statement read.

"It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The letter criticizes Infantino's now scrapped plan to form a subsidiary arm of FIFA (International Federation of Association Football) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors.

It says that even in withdrawing the plan, FIFA "did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong."

It also labels the plan a "fundamental breach of trust" and lambasted Infantino's seemingly unilateral actions in bypassing the executive FIFA Council for his initial proposal and then holding a summit in Morocco with only selected senior figures within the organization.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness," the letter reads.

The statement comes after media reports that UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Infantino during his time at the European confederation. FIFA in response criticized "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims" and said that "it is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."

FIFA have not yet replied to a DW request for comment on the open letter.

What does this change for Infantino?

Were the national federations of the three confederations to fall in line, there would be easily enough votes to oust Infantino at the presidential election in March 2027. FIFA has 211 voting members and thus a presidential candidate in a two-horse race would require 106 votes. UEFA (55 members) AFC (46) and CONCACAF (35) would easily have enough if each confederation's members voted as a bloc.

However, this seems unlikely. While UEFA, who have driven much of the opposition, seem relatively united, the picture in the two other confederations is more mixed. Mexico, one of CONCACAF's most powerful nations and a World Cup 2026 cohost, have backed Infantino while Qatar, who hosted the 2022 World Cup, is one of several Asian nations to have broken ranks.

The South American federation CONMEBOL (10) does not yet have a clear position on Infantino, but one of its most powerful nations, Argentina, have lent Infantino their support. The Oceania federation (11) has also yet to make its position clear.

Perhaps the best news for Infantino was the backing of the African confederation, CAF (54), last week.

A statement from the organization's executive committee said that CAF "unanimously reconfirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino and thanked him for his support for African Football over the years."

Is there a candidate to challenge Infantino?

This is the big question. As it stands, no candidate has stepped forward. Infantino won the last presidential election unopposed and looked likely to do so again next March, until a few weeks ago.

Though the clear positioning of several confederations against Infantino suggests that running unopposed again is now unlikely, a candidate that can unite those federations in opposition to the Swiss administrator is the next step.

"There's such an imperative to get a candidate who could unite the whole world of football, not just Europe in this case," UEFA vice president, Laura McAllister, recently told DW.

"It's not as easy as people might think. The right candidate has to also have the right level of support," McAllister said. "But if we're talking about the right candidate, then I think that person, that man or woman, needs to be somebody who recognizes that we are simply custodians of the sport and that we look after it and hopefully leave it in better health."

What might happen next?

There will no doubt be plenty of backroom talks about finding a candidate and announcing them at the right time. But given that Infantino retains a reasonable amount of support, football's powerbrokers will likely want to ensure whoever they might put up can win. UEFA executives will likely discuss this at the Super Cup (between the winners of last season's Champions League and Europa League) later this week, while other federations will look to do similar.

Looming in early September is the first FIFA tournament since the controversial sell-off plan was announced. The U-20 Women's World Cup is being held in Poland, a UEFA member, and it is not yet clear whether European teams will participate in the tournament with Infantino still in charge.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia
World.content:
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least 13 people and wounded 48 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

Ukraine's military ⁠said ⁠it struck the Taneco oil refinery overnight, adding that a ⁠fire was recorded at the site.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Russia, Ukraine: Deadly drone and missile attacks escalate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.
